en: [The first chapter, the first section:
"Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma. (1.1.1)

[1,ii] The second chapter: On the refutation of the self through the examination of its characteristics. First, the refutation of the self as a substantial entity; second, the refutation of the self as a conceptual designation. First, the refutation of the self as a substantial entity has two parts: first, the refutation of the self as a substance distinct from the aggregates; second, the refutation of the self as a substance identical to the aggregates. First, the refutation of the self as a substance distinct from the aggregates has three parts: first, the refutation by means of logical reasoning; second, the refutation by means of scriptural authority; third, the refutation by means of the consequences of the opponent’s own assertions. First, the refutation by means of logical reasoning has four parts: first, the refutation by means of the reason that it would follow that the agent and the experiencer are different; second, the refutation by means of the reason that it would follow that there is no basis for the conventional designation of "self"; third, the refutation by means of the reason that it would follow that the self is impermanent; fourth, the refutation by means of the reason that it would follow that the self is not the object of the sixth consciousness. First, the refutation by means of the reason that it would follow that the agent and the experiencer are different: If the self were a substance distinct from the aggregates, then the agent and the experiencer would be different. If they were different, then the agent who performs the action would not be the one who experiences the fruit; thus, the agent and the experiencer would be separate entities. This contradicts the world's common understanding and the scriptures of our own school. Therefore, the self is not a substance distinct from the aggregates. Second, the refutation by means of the reason that it would follow that there is no basis for the conventional designation of "self": If the self were a substance distinct from the aggregates, then since the aggregates are multiple and momentary, the self would likewise be multiple and momentary. If this were so, there would be no stable basis for the conventional designation of "self," just as there is no such basis for the designation of "chariot" when the parts are disassembled. Therefore, the self is not a substance distinct from the aggregates. Third, the refutation by means of the reason that it would follow that the self is impermanent: If the self were a substance distinct from the aggregates, then because the aggregates are impermanent, the self would also be impermanent. If this were so, it would contradict the opponent’s own assertion that the self is eternal. Therefore, the self is not a substance distinct from the aggregates. Fourth, the refutation by means of the reason that it would follow that the self is not the object of the sixth consciousness: If the self were a substance distinct from the aggregates, then since the sixth consciousness does not apprehend anything other than the aggregates, the self would not be an object of the sixth consciousness. If this were so, it would contradict the opponent’s own assertion that the self is perceived by the sixth consciousness. Therefore, the self is not a substance distinct from the aggregates. Second, the refutation by means of scriptural authority: As the Blessed One said in the *Sūtra on the Refutation of the Self*: "The self is merely a designation based upon the aggregates; it is neither a substance nor a person. Therefore, the self is not a substance distinct from the aggregates. Third, the refutation by means of the consequences of the opponent’s own assertions: If the self were a substance distinct from the aggregates, then it would follow that the self could exist independently of the aggregates even after death, and it would follow that one could abandon the aggregates while retaining the self. Since these consequences are untenable, the self is not a substance distinct from the aggregates. Second, the refutation of the self as a substance identical to the aggregates has two parts: first, the refutation of the self as identical to a single aggregate; second, the refutation of the self as identical to all the aggregates collectively. First, the refutation of the self as identical to a single aggregate: If the self were identical to a single aggregate, then because the aggregates are five in number, there would be five selves. Furthermore, since the aggregates are momentary, the self would likewise be momentary. Moreover, since the aggregates are material or immaterial, the self would be both material and immaterial. These consequences are all untenable. Therefore, the self is not a substance identical to a single aggregate. Second, the refutation of the self as identical to all the aggregates collectively: If the self were identical to all the aggregates collectively, then because the aggregates are multiple, the self would be multiple. Furthermore, because the aggregates are impermanent, the self would be impermanent. Moreover, because the aggregates are distinct from one another, the self would be fragmented. These consequences are all untenable. Therefore, the self is not a substance identical to all the aggregates collectively. Second, the refutation of the self as a conceptual designation has two parts: first, the refutation of the self as designated by way of identity; second, the refutation of the self as designated by way of dependence. First, the refutation of the self as designated by way of identity: If the self were designated by way of identity with the aggregates, then the terms "self" and "aggregates" would be synonymous. However, in the world, the terms "chariot" and "parts of a chariot" are not synonymous, as the chariot is designated in dependence upon its parts. Therefore, the self is not designated by way of identity with the aggregates. Second, the refutation of the self as designated by way of dependence: If the self were designated by way of dependence upon the aggregates, then it would be like the designation of a "chariot" in dependence upon its parts. In that case, the self would be a mere conceptual construct and would lack any substantial reality. This is acceptable to us, but it contradicts the opponent’s assertion that the self is a real entity. Therefore, the self is not a substance, whether distinct from or identical to the aggregates. It is merely a conceptual designation based upon the aggregates. Thus, the self is refuted. Second, the refutation of the self through the examination of its characteristics has two parts: first, the refutation of the self as a permanent entity; second, the refutation of the self as an impermanent entity. First, the refutation of the self as a permanent entity: If the self were permanent, it would be incapable of performing actions or experiencing results, as a permanent entity cannot undergo change. Furthermore, if the self were permanent, then since the aggregates are impermanent, the self and the aggregates would be entirely distinct, which contradicts the opponent’s own position. Therefore, the self is not a permanent entity. Second, the refutation of the self as an impermanent entity: If the self were impermanent, then it would be subject to arising and ceasing, and there would be no continuity of personal identity. Furthermore, if the self were impermanent, it would be a conditioned phenomenon, and as such, it would be empty of intrinsic nature. Therefore, the self is not an impermanent entity. In conclusion, the self is neither a substance nor a conceptual designation, neither permanent nor impermanent. It is merely a false construction. Thus, the self is thoroughly refuted. [1,ii]

To a certain Brāhmaṇa whose impurities had been removed through the study of the Vedas, this Vedic statement appeared: "Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who exists as the body alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1). Having reflected upon this statement, he approached Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda) and said: "Venerable sir! By this statement, it is declared that there is a means for attaining security for one who has cast off the body; let that be told—what is the means? Then the sage replied: "It is Dharma. Thereupon the Brāhmaṇa asked: "What is Dharma? What is its definition? What are its means? What is its purpose? And whom does it benefit? Therefore, immediately following these questions, in the promise to explain Dharma, the word *atha* (now/then) denotes immediate succession. The word *ataḥ* (hence) also points to the perfection of the disciple's qualities—such as dispassion, wisdom, and the ripening of their discourse—as the cause; because this disciple is endowed with such a perfection of qualities, we shall therefore explain Dharma to him immediately after these questions.
[1,iii] What is dharma? It is said:
“That from which the attainment of worldly prosperity and the supreme good results is dharma. (1.1.2)

Since actions such as sacrifices and the worship of deities—which are accomplished by means of clarified butter, flowers, and so forth—perish at that very moment and are thus incapable of yielding a fruit at a later time, one must understand that *dharma* is that cause from which prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) arise. Prosperity consists in the attainment of a desirable body in the worlds of Brahmā and other realms, as well as the cessation of misfortune. The supreme good is liberation (*mokṣa*), which consists in the absence of the specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*) of the self.
If it is asked how such a defined *dharma* is known, [the answer is]: from the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*). To explain how its authority is established, he says:
“From his word, the authority of the sacred tradition [is established].

(1.1.3) [2,ii] The word *tat* (that) refers to Hiraṇyagarbha; for since he possesses golden seed (*hiraṇya-retas*), the Blessed Lord Maheśvara himself is meant. Since being spoken by a trustworthy person (*āpta*) is pervaded by truthfulness, the authority of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is here established on the grounds that it was spoken by the trustworthy Hiraṇyagarbha. Furthermore, God has been established through the inference that because bodies, worlds, and so forth are effects, like a jar, they must have an intelligent agent as their creator.

[2,iii] The nature of *dharma* and its characteristics have been explained. Now we shall describe its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), namely substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*). Among these, it is said:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind are the substances" (VS 1.1.4).

[2.iv] They are substances because of their connection with substantiality (*dravyatva*). It is earth because of its connection with earthness (*pṛthivītva*); the designations of water and so forth are likewise. The word "thus" (*iti*) is for the purpose of indicating that there are exactly nine substances and no more.
Thus have the substances been enumerated. What, then, are the qualities? He says:

"Color, taste, smell, touch, numbers, dimensions, separateness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, cognitions, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, and effort—these are the qualities" (1.1.5).

These seventeen qualities, beginning with form (*rūpa*) and explicitly mentioned, as well as those included by the word "and" (*ca*), are understood to be gravity (*gurutva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), viscidity (*sneha*), latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and sound (*śabda*). These will be explained in due course below.
Furthermore, he asks: "What, then, are the actions? and says:
“Throwing upwards, throwing downwards, contraction, expansion, and going—these are the actions. (1.1.6)

<3> These very five types of action (*karman*) are to be understood. By the mention of "going" (*gamana*), "whirling," "shaking," and so forth are included. Thus, substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*) have been enumerated. Following that, generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) will also be discussed. Thus, the thorough knowledge of the similarities and differences among these six categories, by way of perceiving the defects of sense objects, leads to the arising of dispassion; when this occurs, it serves as the cause of *dharma* for the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Furthermore, their status as causes of *dharma* for the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) is as follows: for Earth, "one should sacrifice on level ground"; for other substances, "it carries water downward," and so forth, according to their respective natures. For qualities, [the injunction is] "one should sacrifice a black animal," and so forth. For actions, [the injunction is] "one threshes rice," and so forth.

[3,i] Since substances (*dravya*) and the other categories possess known similarities and dissimilarities, and because they are the causes of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), he first states their similarity: “Existent, non-eternal, possessing substance, effect, cause, and possessing generality and particularity— this is the common characteristic of substances, qualities, and motions” (1.1.7).

[3,ii] The second section: the detailed explanation of the characteristics of the three natures. This has two parts: first, the general presentation; second, the detailed explanation. First, the general presentation: "The imagined nature is that which is grasped by the ignorant as being external objects, while the dependent nature is the manifestation of those very objects within consciousness. This means that the imagined nature refers to the objects such as form and so forth, which are grasped by the ignorant as being external to consciousness; the dependent nature refers to the manifestation of those very objects within consciousness itself. Second, the detailed explanation has two parts: first, the detailed explanation of the imagined nature; second, the detailed explanation of the dependent nature. First, the detailed explanation of the imagined nature: "The imagined nature is the aspect of the object, because it is not established as a real entity. This means that the imagined nature is the aspect of the object, because it is not established as a real entity. Second, the detailed explanation of the dependent nature: "The dependent nature is the aspect of the subject, because it arises from conditions. This means that the dependent nature is the aspect of the subject, because it arises from conditions. It is called "dependent" because it arises in dependence upon causes and conditions. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "The dependent nature is the mind and mental factors of the three realms, which arise from the seeds of false discrimination. This means that the dependent nature refers to the mind and mental factors of the three realms, which arise from the seeds of false discrimination. False discrimination refers to the seeds of the dependent nature; because they are false, they are called "false," and because they discriminate, they are called "discrimination. These seeds give rise to the mind and mental factors of the three realms, which constitute the dependent nature. Second, explaining its synonyms: "It is also called 'the storehouse consciousness,' 'the appropriating consciousness,' and 'the fundamental consciousness. This means that the dependent nature is also called the storehouse consciousness, the appropriating consciousness, and the fundamental consciousness. Third, explaining its divisions: "Furthermore, it is divided into two types: the afflicted and the pure. This means that the dependent nature is further divided into two types: the afflicted and the pure. Fourth, explaining its establishment: "It is established as the dependent nature because it arises in dependence upon other conditions. This means that it is established as the dependent nature because it arises in dependence upon other conditions. It is called "dependent" because it arises in dependence upon other conditions. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "The perfected nature is the absence of duality in the dependent nature. This means that the perfected nature is the absence of duality in the dependent nature. Duality refers to the grasper and the grasped; their absence is called "non-dual. Because it is non-dual, it is called "perfected"; because it is the ultimate reality, it is called "nature. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is eternally free from the two kinds of error. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is eternally free from the two kinds of error. The two kinds of error refer to the errors of existence and non-existence. Because it is eternally free from these two kinds of error, it is called "perfected. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the ultimate reality. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the ultimate reality. It is called "perfected" because it is the ultimate reality. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the noble ones' wisdom. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of the noble ones' wisdom. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of the noble ones' wisdom. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the non-conceptual wisdom. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of non-conceptual wisdom. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of non-conceptual wisdom. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of equality. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of equality. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of the wisdom of equality. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of discernment. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of discernment. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of the wisdom of discernment. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of accomplishment. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of accomplishment. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of the wisdom of accomplishment. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of subsequent attainment. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of subsequent attainment. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of the wisdom of subsequent attainment. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of the path. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of the path. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of the wisdom of the path. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of the fruit. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of the fruit. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of the wisdom of the fruit. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of liberation. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of liberation. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of the wisdom of liberation. It is called "nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all phenomena. Furthermore, this is explained through four aspects: first, explaining its characteristic; second, explaining its synonyms; third, explaining its divisions; fourth, explaining its establishment. First, explaining its characteristic: "It is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of the dharmadhātu. This means that it is the perfected nature because it is the object of the wisdom of the dharmadhātu. It is called "perfected" because it is the object of the wisdom of the dharmadhātu. It

"Existence (sat), substance (dravya), and existence as a cow (san goḥ) and existence as action (sat karma)"—thus, existence is common to all three. Likewise, impermanence is common to them, with the exception of ether and the like. "Possessing substance" means possessing an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa); this is common to them, excluding atoms, ether, and so forth. "Being an effect" means coming into being after not having existed; likewise, this is common to them, with the exception of eternal substances. "Being a cause" means being a generator of effects; this is common to the three. Earth and the other [elements] are the inherent causes of substances, qualities, and actions; ether and the others are the inherent causes of qualities; and the mind and the final parts of a substance are the inherent causes of qualities and actions. As for qualities: color, taste, smell, non-hot touch, number, dimension, singularity, separateness, viscidity, and sound are non-inherent causes. Cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impression (bhāvanā) are efficient causes. Conjunction, disjunction, heat, gravity, fluidity, and speed are causes in both ways (inherent and efficient). Priority, posteriority, duality, dual separateness, spherical dimension, and so forth, are not causes. Actions are non-inherent causes in conjunctions and disjunctions. Universals are those such as substantiality (dravyatva) and the like, and particulars are those [ultimate differentiators]; thus, "possessing universals and particulars" is common to the three.
[3,iii] When the identity of the three is established, their distinction is stated. Thus it says: “Substances originate another substance. (1.1.8)

[3, iv] Regarding the analysis of the compound as "in a substance" (*dravye*) and "substances" (*dravyāṇi*), one [type of substance] is non-productive. Substances that are inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) initiate a product-substance distinct from themselves. However, substances such as space (*ākāśa*) and other ultimate composite substances (*antyāvayavidravya*) do not initiate a substance, because only two or more causes of a similar class—possessing corporeality, motion, color, and so forth—initiate an effect. Such is not the case for space and the like. Furthermore, the mind (*manas*) is not a cause of substance because it lacks tangibility, and ultimate composite substances are not observed [to produce further effects].
“Qualities and other qualities” (1.1.9).

The terms “two qualities” (*guṇau*) and “qualities” (*guṇāḥ*) are to be understood as before. For example, the color and other qualities of the threads produce, within the cloth-substance which inheres in those same substrates, qualities such as color that are distinct from themselves.
[4,iii] “Action is not found to be accomplishable by action. (1.1.10) [4,iv]

Action is not produced by action, because we observe the cessation of actions. For if action were produced by action, there would be no perception of a substance that is devoid of action at the commencement of actions. Thus, some substances would be initiators and others would not; some qualities would be causes and others would not; yet actions themselves would never be the cause of action—this is the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
He states another dissimilarity:
“Substance is non-contradictory to its effects and non-contradictory to its causes.

Destruction is opposition (virodha), which is a form of obstruction (pratibandha). In some cases, an effect such as a substance does not oppose its cause-substance, nor its inherent (samavāyin) or non-inherent (asamavāyin) causes. For example: a finger-substance, which is the effect, is not opposed by the action intended to produce a two-finger-length [space], nor by the conjunction produced by that action, nor by the resulting two-finger-length [space]; nor is it opposed by its inherent and non-inherent causes, namely the joints and their respective conjunctions. Likewise, the mind and ultimate composite substances are not opposed by their effects, such as qualities and actions; and ether and other eternal substances are not opposed by their qualities. Because these are eternal, there is no opposition with respect to their causes.
[4,vii] “There is merit in both ways.

[Qualities] are both non-contradictory and contradictory with respect to effects, causes, both, and neither. In substances such as atoms, dyads, and so forth, up to the ultimate composite substances, qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and the rest are, as the case may be, non-contradictory with effects, both [cause and effect], and causes. Color, taste, smell, and touch, when not standing in a cause-and-effect relationship, are non-contradictory with one another. Contradictory [qualities] are: initial, middle, and final sounds with respect to effects and both [cause and effect]; the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) with respect to its effect; speed and effort with respect to conjunction with a tangible substance; conjunction and disjunction; pleasure and pain; and desire and aversion, which are mutually contradictory even when not standing in a cause-and-effect relationship. Furthermore, cognition is contradictory with the counter-agents to the stream of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and mental impression is contradictory with cognition, pleasure, pain, and so forth; this is to be understood according to the circumstances.
[5,i] “Action is that which is opposed to its own effect.

Among the effects— conjunction (*saṃyoga*), disjunction (*vibhāga*), and impression (*saṃskāra*)— action is contradicted by conjunction alone, not by disjunction or impression, because that would entail the non-production of conjunction.
[5, iii] There is also another point of dissimilarity:
“Possessing action, possessing quality, and being an inherent cause—this is the definition of substance. (1.1.14) [5,iv]

Action (*karma*), such as throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and so forth, is that in which action exists by way of inherence (*samavāya*) according to possibility; it is "possessing action" (*kriyāvat*). This excludes space, time, direction, and the self (*ātman*). Quality (*guṇa*), such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, is that in which qualities exist according to possibility; it is "possessing quality" (*guṇavat*). Inherence (*samavāya*) is that from which the notion "here" arises with respect to things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relation of the supported and the support. That which possesses this [inherence] is "possessing inherence" (*samavāyi*), and it is precisely that which is the cause; or rather, it is the cause of the effect that possesses inherence. In this regard, earth and the other [elements] are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the three—substance, quality, and action; space and the others are [the inherent causes] of qualities; and the mind (*manas*) is [the inherent cause] of qualities and actions within a substance consisting of the ultimate atom (*antyāvayavin*).
[5,v] “Residing in a substance, being devoid of qualities, and not being a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent— this is the definition of a quality. (1.1.15) [5,vi]

That which rests upon substance is "substance-dependent" (*dravyāśrayī*); it is "without qualities" (*nirguṇa*), meaning devoid of qualities. It is "independent" (*anapekṣa*) in being a non-cause of conjunctions and disjunctions; whereas that which is dependent (*sāpekṣa*) is a cause. Thus it is said: the conjunction of two fingers, when about to produce the conjunction of the space between them, depends upon the production of the two-fingered space; the mutual disjunction of the two fingers, with respect to the disjunction from the space between them, depends upon the destruction of the effect. In this way, a quality characterized by conjunction and disjunction is a dependent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions. [5.vii]
“Action is defined as that which has a single substance as its substratum, is devoid of qualities, and is an independent cause with respect to conjunctions and disjunctions.

(1.1.16) [5,viii] This action has one substance as its locus, not two; or rather, it exists in only one substance, thus it is "single-substantiated" (*ekadravya*). It is "devoid of qualities" (*aguṇa*) because it possesses no qualities. With respect to its effects—conjunctions and disjunctions—it is an "independent cause" (*anapekṣaṃ kāraṇam*) because, having separated its own substratum from one thing and joined it with another substratum, it acts without depending on anything else for the production or destruction of those conjunctions and disjunctions.
[5,ix] There is also another point of dissimilarity: “Substance is the common cause of substances, qualities, and actions. (1.1.17)

[6,i] The word "sāmānya" (common) is a synonym for "samāna" (equal/common). Earth and the other [elements] are the common cause of three [categories]. Although ether and the others are causes only of qualities (*guṇa*), because each one possesses multiple qualities, ether and the others are a common cause with respect to qualities; the mind (*manas*) is [the cause] of qualities and actions (*karman*) in the case of the final composite substance.
“Likewise, quality [is a cause].

(1.1.18) [6, iii] From the statements, “Substance [is the cause] of conjunctions” (1.1.25), “Because of the appearance of another quality due to contact with fire” (7.1.5, 6), and “Action in the hand [arises] from conjunction with the self and from effort” (5.1.1), it follows that conjunction alone is the common cause of substances, qualities, and actions, and no other quality is so. For instance: from the conjunction of a tuft of cotton with a swift-moving tuft of cotton, there arises action; then a substance consisting of two tufts of cotton; and therein, a large dimension (*mahat-parimāṇa*) is produced, as well as other qualities as appropriate.
[6,iv] “Action is that which possesses conjunctions and disjunctions.
Having separated its own substratum from one thing, it joins it with another substratum; therefore, action is the common cause of conjunctions and disjunctions.
[6, vi] "Not [the cause] of substances, because of their distinctness" (1.1.20).

[6,vii] If action were indeed the cause of substance, then even after conjunction has been produced, it would not cease; however, since we perceive conjunction alone once the action has ceased, we conclude that "action is not the cause of substance.
[6,viii]

“Because of the difference in properties from the qualities, action is not the cause of actions” (1.1.21). Gravity, fluidity, impulse, pressure, and conjunction with that which is conjoined are causes of action both in their own substratum and in another substratum; however, effort and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) are causes of action only in another substratum. In that regard, action is not the cause of action in its own substratum, because it would follow that motionless substances could not be perceived. Nor is it the cause in another substratum, because [action there] is already brought about by the conjunction itself. Therefore, because of this difference in properties from these qualities which are causes of action, action is not the cause of action.
[6,x] Another point of dissimilarity:
"Among substances, substance and action are common. (1.1.22)
[6,xi] Among homogeneous things, whether two or many substances, one substance is their common effect, just as cloth is the common effect of threads.
[6,xii]
“Numbers beginning with duality, as well as separateness, conjunction, and disjunction” (1.1.23).

Duality is a commonality (*sāmānya*) that is an effect produced by two substances; likewise for trinity in three, and so forth. Similarly, there is dual-separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*) and so on. Conjunction belongs to two substances that are being conjoined, and disjunction belongs to those that are being separated. Because these reside in more than one [substratum], they possess commonality (*samānyatva*).
“Because of non-inherence, there is no common effect of action” (1.1.24).
Since the inherence of a single action in multiple substances is denied, there is no common effect of action for two or more substances.
[7,iii] “Substance is that which possesses conjunctions.
The substance is the common effect of two or many non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) in the form of conjunctions (*saṃyoga*), just as cloth is the effect of the conjunctions of threads.
[7,v] “From colors, color [arises]. (1.1.26)

[7, vi] The common effect is the form residing in the substance that is the effect, which belongs to two or many forms that are causes; for example, the form of a jar is the common effect of the forms of its shards, and the same applies to taste and so forth.
[7, vii]
“Throwing upward results from gravity, effort, and conjunction.

(1.1.27) [7, viii] Because the rays of the sun lack gravity, because there is no such effort in the case of a mountain, and because a clod of earth is not conjoined with the hand, there is no throwing upward; thus, gravity and the other factors have throwing upward as their common effect.
[7,ix] “The conjunctions and disjunctions of actions. (1.1.28) [7,x]

Those conjunctions and disjunctions produced by both [types of] action constitute the common effect of actions. [7,xi] “When the cause is the same, it has been stated that among substances and actions, action is not a cause [of another action]. (1.1.29)

[7,xii] In that section where the common cause of substances (*dravya*) and so forth was described, regarding that general nature of causality, since it was stated that action (*karman*) is not a cause for substances and actions, therefore these [substances and qualities] also do not constitute its common effect. Thus, it is established that substances, qualities, and actions are distinct. <End of the First Āhnika of the First Adhyāya>
<The Second Daily Lesson of the First Chapter> [8,i] “From the absence of the cause follows the absence of the effect. (1.2.1)

[8, ii] The terms "effect" (*kārya*) and "cause" (*kāraṇa*) were mentioned previously; in order to define them, he says: that in the absence of which the effect-substance, such as a cloth, is not produced—whether it be the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) such as the threads or the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) such as their conjunctions—or that by whose destruction it perishes, is the "cause"; anything else is the "effect.
[8, iii]
"But the absence of the cause does not follow from the absence of the effect" (1.2.2).
Furthermore, upon the non-production of a cloth or the like, there is no non-production of the substance— the threads or their conjunctions.
[8,v] The three categories beginning with generality (*sāmānya*), which were mentioned as incidental, have been discussed; therein, he explains generality:
"Generality and particularity depend upon cognition" (1.2.3).

[8, vi] With reference to the cognition "cow, cow" which persists among individual objects that are distinct, and with reference to the cognition "this is different from that" which excludes them from one another, there is the universal (*sāmānya*) in dependence on the cognition of persistence, and the particular (*viśeṣa*) in dependence on the cognition of exclusion.
[8, vii]
“Existence (*bhāva*) is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*).
(1.2.4) Existence, which is being (*sattā*), is indeed a universal because it persists through all three categories— substance and the rest— and is not a particular (*viśeṣa*).
[8,ix] “Substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness are both generalities and particulars. (1.2.5) [8,x]

Since there is a recurring cognition (*anuvṛttibuddhi*) as "substance, substance" with respect to earth and the other [elements], and "quality, quality" with respect to color and the other [qualities], and "action, action" with respect to throwing upward and the other [actions], these are the universals (*sāmānya*) of substantiality, quality-ness, and action-ness; and because they are excluded from one another, they are also particulars (*viśeṣa*).
[8,xi] "Except for the ultimate particulars. (1.2.6)

[8,xii] Existing by way of inherence (*samavāya*) in eternal substances such as atoms (*paramāṇu*), space (*ākāśa*), and so forth—which possess equal forms and qualities—the *viśeṣas* (particularities) are the causes of the cognition of absolute exclusion, "this is different from that," for those who perceive them; they are called *viśeṣas* because they distinguish those [substances]. Thus have the *viśeṣas* been explained.
Existence (sattā), however, is that from which [the notion] "it exists" arises with respect to substances, qualities, and actions. (1.2.7) [9,ii]
That from which the cognition "existent, existent" arises with respect to the three categories— substance and so forth— when they are differentiated, is *sattā* (existence).
If it is argued that its destruction follows from the destruction of its substratum, we say no, because:
“Existence (*sattā*) is a distinct entity from substance, quality, and action” (1.2.8).
Because existence is separate from substances and the other categories, it does not perish when substances and the like perish.
The reasoning for its distinction from substance and the other categories is as follows:
“Because it inheres in a single substance, it is not a substance. (1.2.9)

[9, vi] Substances such as atoms and space are non-substances (*adravya*) because they lack causal substances; or alternatively, substances such as jars are "multiple-substance" (*anekadravya*) because they are joined with inherent causal substances. Existence (*sattā*), however, is not a substance, because it exists by being fully present in each individual [substance] and thus possesses only a single substance.
[9, vii]
“Because it exists in qualities and actions, it is neither quality nor action” (1.2.10).
Since qualities do not subsist in qualities and actions do not subsist in actions, and since existence (*sattā*) subsists in both qualities and actions, existence is neither a quality nor an action.
“And because of the absence of both generality and particularity. (1.2.11) [9,x]

If existence (*sattā*) were one of the categories such as substance (*dravya*), then just as in the case of substances and so forth, the general-particulars (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) would subsist in existence as well. But this is not the case. Therefore, existence is not substance, quality, or action.
[9,xi] "Substantiality has been stated [to exist] by virtue of having a single substance" (1.2.12).

[9,xii] Just as existence (*sattā*) is not a substance because it exists in its entirety within each individual substance, so too substantiality (*dravyatva*) is not a substance because it resides in a single substance.
[9,xiii]
“And because of the absence of commonalities and particularities” (1.2.13).

Just as in the case of substances and so forth, if some commonality-particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) from among [the categories such as] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so on were to reside in substantiality itself, then it would follow that substance, quality, or action would exist [within substantiality]. Therefore, substances and the other categories do not constitute substantiality.
“Because it exists in qualities, it is called a quality. (1.2.14)
Because qualities do not reside in qualities, and because the state of being a quality (*guṇatva*) resides in qualities, it is therefore not a quality.
[10,iii] "And because of the absence of commonalities and particularities" (1.2.15).

[10,iv] If "quality-ness" (guṇatva) were a substance or an action, then "substance-ness" (dravyatva) or "action-ness" (karmatva) would be its specific universals (sāmānyaviśeṣa). But this is not the case. Therefore, quality-ness is neither a substance nor an action.
“Because it exists in the object, it is called ‘object-ness’” (1.2.16).
Since object-ness resides in the object, and since the object does not reside in the object, the object is not itself object-ness.
“And because of the absence of both generality and particularity. (1.2.17) [10,viii]

If action were either substance or quality, then it would possess the nature of substance or quality; therefore, action is neither substance nor quality. [10, ix] "Because there is no distinction in the mark of existence and because there is an absence of a specific mark, Being is one. (1.2.18)

[10,x] By the word "one" (eka), non-difference is expressed, not number. A "mark" (liṅga) is that by which something is marked; it is a cognition (pratyaya). Since existence (sattā) is cognized by the cognition "existent, existent," and because that [cognition] is undifferentiated everywhere and there is no differentiated cognition [of it], existence is non-different.

[The First Daily Lesson of the Second Chapter] [11,i] Thus, since the plurality of substances and other categories has been established, and since earth and the others would consequently appear to be one due to the non-difference of their definition as substance, he states their difference through the distinction of their definitions:
“Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch.

(2.1.1) These—color, taste, smell, and touch—are its specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*); others, however, are number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, occasional fluidity, and momentum. Color consists of white and so forth; taste consists of sweet and so forth; smell is both fragrant and foul; its touch, being neither hot nor cold, is produced by maturation (*pākaja*). Its effects are both external and internal.
[11,iii] "Water possesses color, taste, and touch; it is fluid and viscous. (2.1.2) [11,iv]

Their color, taste, and touch are exclusively white, sweet, and cold. They are liquid; this refers to their natural fluidity (*sāṃsiddhika-dravatva*). They are unctuous; this refers to their viscidity (*sneha*). They also possess number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, weight, and momentum. Their effects are as previously described. [11,v] "Fire possesses color and touch. (2.1.3)

[11, vi] Its color is radiant and white; its touch is exclusively hot. It possesses number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, occasional fluidity, and momentum. Its effects are as previously described.
“Air possesses touch.

(2.1.4) [11, viii] Its touch is neither hot nor cold and is not produced by heating. It also possesses number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, gravity, and faculty. Its effects are as previously described. Its bodies, such as those of terrestrial beings and others, exist in the worlds of earth and so forth.
[11,ix] “They do not exist in space. (2.1.5) [11,x]

Those qualities—color, taste, smell, and touch—do not exist in space (*ākāśa*). Its qualities are sound, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction. [11,xi] “The fluidity of earthly substances such as clarified butter, lac, and beeswax, resulting from contact with fire, is a commonality with water. (2.1.6)
<12> *Madhūcchiṣṭa* is beeswax. That fluidity which arises from contact with fire in clarified butter, lac, and beeswax is the similarity of earth with water.
[12,i] “The fluidity of tin, lead, iron, silver, and gold—which are fiery in nature—that arises from contact with fire is their commonality with water. (2.1.7)
[12,ii] Furthermore, that fluidity which arises in these luminous substances through contact with fire is the common property of light in relation to water.
“Having horns, having a hump, having a tail with a tuft at the end, and having a dewlap—these are the observed marks for the nature of a cow.

The Sūtra is for the sake of providing an illustration. "In 'cowness'" (*gotve*) means an individual instance delimited by cowness. It has horns, a hump, and a dewlap; thus it is "horned," "humped," and "dewlapped. By the word *prānta*, the hip region is meant; by the word *vāladhi*—meaning that in which the tail-hairs (*bāla*) are placed—the tail is meant. Thus, "having a tail at its end" (*prāntevāladhiḥ*). Although words such as "horned" and so forth denote the possessor of those attributes, it is the properties (*dharmāḥ*) themselves that are designated through their operation upon the object.

Just as, when the individual cow is not perceived, the horns and other such features— being apprehended in some way— are seen to be a logical mark (*liṅga*) that leads to inference, so too is "touch" [according to 2.1.9].
Touch, being perceived, leads to the inference of air because it would be impossible for it to exist without a substratum.
[12.vii] "And since touch does not belong to those things that are seen, air has an unperceived mark. (2.1.10)

[12.viii] If this touch belonging to earth and the other elements were indeed [identical to them], we would perceive it together with their odors, tastes, and forms; but since this is not the case, it is therefore the mark (liṅga) of air, which is distinct from earth and the others.
“Because it does not possess [other] substances, it is a substance” (2.1.11).

That wind which has the nature of an atom is indeed a substance because it does not possess [other] substances—that is, because it is devoid of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). For a substance is either without [further] substances or composed of multiple substances.
[12,xi] “Because it possesses action and because it possesses qualities.

(2.1.12) Since the definition of a substance (*dravya*) is given as “that which possesses action and possesses qualities” (1.1.14), that great air (*mahān vāyuḥ*), in which actions and qualities are inherent (*samaveta*), is also a substance.
[13,i] “Its permanence has been stated by virtue of its being devoid of constituent substance.
It has been stated that air characterized by atoms is eternal because it lacks substantiality and is devoid of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
[13,iii] “The mingling of air with air is the mark of its plurality” (2.1.14).

[13.iv] Or, in the case of wind moving horizontally, upward movement occurs through the condensation of wind and its conjunction with another wind; from that upward movement follows conjunction, and from conjunction, the multiplicity of wind is inferred.
But is it not the case that:
"In the case of air, since there is no perception when there is sense-object contact, no perceived mark (liṅga) exists" (2.1.15)?

Just as when there is contact between the eye and a cow, such that "this is a cow," the horns and so forth are seen through perception as being connected to it and thus sometimes serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*); it is not the same way that when there is contact between the skin and air, a touch is perceived through perception as a quality of that [air] such that one could, by means of that [perception], sometimes infer the air which is not being perceived.

If it is argued that because this touch has properties different from the touches of earth and so forth, and because a touch cannot exist without a substratum, air must be its substratum; [the response follows].
“And from the ‘inference based on general observation’ (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa), there is no distinction.

(2.1.16) [13.viii] Since even ether and the other [elements] are imperceptible, the specific distinction that “this touch belongs to air alone” cannot be understood from this inference based on general observation. If it is argued that there would be an obstruction of entities if all-pervading things possessed touch, then how is it known—given this [objection]—that this touch belongs only to air as it is recognized by you, and not to a tenth substance?
“Therefore, it is based on scripture.
Therefore, the statement "air exists" is merely a traditional report based on scripture; this is the meaning.
[13,xi] This is not so.

“However, the act of naming is a mark of those superior to us” (2.1.18). The Lord Maheśvara, who is superior to people such as ourselves by virtue of his knowledge and other qualities, applies names to the nine substances; this is a mark of their existence, because he does not provide a name for a tenth. Therefore, there are only nine substances. Consequently, touch belongs to air alone. In the phrase “those superior to us,” the plural number is used for honor.
How is this known? It is said:
“Because the act of naming is preceded by direct perception. (2.1.19)

[14, ii] For people form designations while perceiving objects through direct perception; this is observed in the case of giving a name to a child, and indeed these designations have been so formed. Therefore, we consider that there exists a Blessed One who is superior to us, a direct witness even of those things imperceptible to people like ourselves, by whom these designations and so forth were established.
“Going out and entering are the marks of space” (2.1.20).

That which constitutes a person’s going out and entering through doors and the like, and not through walls and such, is caused by space; therefore, going out and entering are the marks of space. For space is indeed the absence of material form (*mūrta*).
That is not so,
because: "That is not a valid mark [for the existence of substance], because action possesses only a single substance" (2.1.21).

[14, vi] Since actions such as going out (*niṣkramaṇa*) reside in the person, and because it has been stated that "action resides in a single substance" and space is devoid of action, how could that [action] cause space to move? It cannot, due to the lack of a connection.

If it is argued that just as the falling of a clod of earth is the mark (*liṅga*) of gravity, so too the exiting [of sound] from the person (*puruṣa*) is the mark of space (*ākāśa*), we say: no, "because of the dissimilarity with the postulation of another cause" (2.1.22).
[14.viii]

It has been stated that gravity is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of action; let that be inferred. However, it is not logical for space (*ākāśa*) to possess the status of a non-inherent cause, because space—due to its eternity, substantiality, and independence—is dissimilar to gravity and other such non-inherent causes.
As for what was said, "And emergence is due to the action of space, by means of a door and so forth," that is not correct.
“From conjunction, there is the cessation of action” (2.1.23).

[14,x] Due to the conjunction of the body—the substratum of action—with a tangible substance such as a wall, the act of exiting ceases; this is not, however, because of the absence of space (*ākāśa*), for since it is omnipresent, it exists even there. Therefore, space is known solely through the inferential mark of sound.
If it is argued that sound is a quality belonging only to the causes such as drums and the like, we say no;
for "a quality in the effect is seen to be preceded by a quality in the cause, and because no other effect [of sound] appears, sound is not a quality of those things that possess touch" (2.1.24).
