In this system, those specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of tangible substances (*sparśavat*) which are perceptible by a single sense organ are produced in the effect by means of the qualities of their causes. However, no part of sound is perceived as inhering in the parts of a drum, like the flour and other ingredients in a cake. Therefore, because it does not have the qualities of its cause as its antecedent, sound is not a specific quality of a tangible substance. Furthermore, whatever is a specific quality of a tangible substance is observed to be perceived throughout the duration of that effect; but sound is not like this, and thus it is not a specific quality of a tangible substance. Moreover, a specific quality of a tangible substance is initiated in an effect that has been begun by the qualities of its causes; yet we do not perceive any such effect being produced when one sound initiates another sound. Therefore, because no other effect manifests, sound is not a specific quality of a tangible substance.
[15,iii] “Because it inheres in something else and because it is perceptible, it is neither a quality of the self nor a quality of the mind. (2.1.25) [15,iv]

"Elsewhere" means "externally. Indeed, those qualities that belong to the self, such as pleasure and so forth, are perceived within the body; sound is not like this, because it is perceived externally by many people. Furthermore, a quality of the self is not perceivable by an external sense organ, whereas this [sound] is perceptible by the auditory organ (*śrotra*); therefore, it is not a quality of the self. For this very reason—because it is perceived externally and because it is perceptible by an external sense organ—it is not a quality of the mind (*manas*). And because it is perceptible by the auditory organ, it does not belong to space (*dik*) or time (*kāla*). Therefore, being a quality...
“The mark of space is sound.
(2.1.26) Therefore, sound, when perceived, leads to the inference of space.
[15,vii] “Substantiality and permanence are explained by [the case of] air. (2.1.27) [15,viii]

Just as air, being composed of atoms and lacking constituent parts (*adravyavat*), is a substance and eternal, so too is space a substance and eternal due to the absence of causal substances. [15, ix] “Reality [is established] by its existence. (2.1.28)

[15,x] Just as there is only one entity because there is no distinction in its characteristic marks and because there is an absence of specific characteristic marks, so too is space one because there is no distinction in its characteristic mark— the auditory perception— and because there is an absence of specific characteristic marks.
<Thus ends the first daily lesson of the second chapter.>

[The Second Āhnika of the Second Chapter] As for what was stated—that "the specific qualities of tangible substances do not initiate [their own kind of] quality in the effect-substance they have begun, whereas sound initiates sound in a substance that has not been begun"—that is incorrect; for even in a different substance produced from a flower and a cloth, the fragrance of the flower initiates fragrance in the cloth, and likewise, heat [initiates heat] in water. It is replied:
[16,ii] “When there is contact between a flower and a cloth, the non-appearance of another odor in the cloth is the mark of the absence of odor in it. (2.2.1) [16,iii]

Indeed, when a cloth is joined with a flower, no fragrance is produced by the fragrance of the flower alone, because the fragrance of the cloth also exists; we would perceive a distinct, separate fragrance produced from both the fragrance of the flower and the fragrance of the cloth, but this is not the case, for we perceive only the fragrance of the flower. Therefore, the claim that "when the effect has not yet begun, the fragrance is produced by the fragrance of the flower" is incorrect, as it would entail the presence of a different fragrance altogether.
By this, the heat in water is also explained. (2.2.2)

[16,v] When water comes into contact with fire, the non-production of a distinct touch is the mark of the absence of heat; furthermore, the heat in water does not persist as long as the substance itself. The perception of odor and touch occurs through inherence in the conjoined, due to the transfer of subtle floral particles into the cloth and of fiery particles into the water.

But surely color and other qualities do not persist as long as the substance itself in cloth and water, because one’s own smell and cold touch are not perceived at the time when the smell of a flower and the touch of heat are perceived. No; for it is said: "Smell is established in earth" (2.2.3).
Even when situated in an earthen garment, its own fragrance is not perceived because it is overwhelmed by the fragrance of the flower. Furthermore, [16.viii]...
“Heat resides in fire.
(2.2.4) [16, ix] Heat is established in fire alone; it does not transfer into water.
Likewise, at the time of perceiving heat, there is "coldness in water" (2.2.5).

[17,ii] Due to the penetration of the constituent parts of fire and through the relation of inherence in a conjoined substrate, even though coldness is not perceived in water despite its presence, it remains established there; it is simply not perceived because it is overwhelmed.
Time is now described:
"The marks of time are 'the other,' 'the further,' 'simultaneous,' 'non-simultaneous,' 'long,' and 'quick'" (2.2.6).

These—namely, the notions of priority (*paratva*), posteriority (*aparatva*), simultaneity, and so forth—are the marks (*liṅga*) of time (*kāla*). In this regard, when a youth is conjoined with a remote spatial point and the cognition of priority arises, and an elder is conjoined with a proximate spatial point and the cognition of posteriority arises, that causal factor by which—upon considering such traits as black hair in the youth and wrinkles or grey hair in the elder—the cognition of posteriority arises in the youth and the cognition of priority arises in the elder, is time. Likewise, among agents performing similar actions, that from which the cognition arises—"they act simultaneously" or "they act non-simultaneously"—is time. Similarly, when many actions such as placing a pot on the stove proceed in a continuous series toward a single result called *odana* (rice), while the agent remains the same, that from which the cognitions "this was done long ago" and "this was done quickly" arise is time. Its qualities are number (*saṃkhyā*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and disjunction (*vibhāga*).
Furthermore: "Substantiality and permanence are explained by [the discussion of] air" (2.2.7).
Because it lacks constituent substance, time possesses substantiality and permanence, just like atoms and air.
“Reality [is established] by means of existence.

(2.2.8) Just as there is one single existence because there is no distinction in its characteristic marks and because there is an absence of specific characteristic marks, so too there is one single time because there is no distinction in its characteristic marks and because there is an absence of specific characteristic marks.
[17,ix] To the question, "If time is one, how can there be designations such as the time of commencement and so forth? he says:
"Its plurality is due to specific effects" (2.2.9).

[17,x] *Kārya* is action (*kriyā*). Having observed the actions of beginning, persistence, and destruction of an entity permeated by a specific action, one employs designations such as "the time of beginning" and so forth, by metaphorically attributing multiplicity even to a single time.
Is it not the case that time is merely action? Why? Because the marks of time are absent in eternal things and present in non-eternal things. (2.2.10) [18, ii]

If time were eternal and distinct from action, then the marks of time would appear even in eternal things such as space; however, they occur only in impermanent things. Therefore, time is a limit (*avadhi*) only with respect to things being produced. Thus, action itself is time. This is not so, because the marks of time occur in impermanent things subsequent to the production of the entity, and not because action is time.
As for those [marks]:
“[The term] ‘time’ is a designation for the cause.

(Pāṇini 2.2.11) Since these marks of time cannot exist without a basis, and since they must have action as their basis, one would say “it is done” (*kṛtam*) rather than “simultaneously” (*yugapat*). Therefore, that which is the cause of these [marks] is designated by the name “time.”
“The mark of direction is that from which one says, ‘this is from here. (2.2.12)

Taking a corporeal substance as a limit, that from which this cognition arises—such as "this is to the east of that"—is the mark (liṅga) of direction. Its qualities are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction.
Furthermore:
“Substantiality and eternity have been explained by [the case of] air.
(2.2.13) Because it is devoid of constituent substances, the substantiality and eternity of space are like those of air.
“Reality is by way of its own being. (2.2.14)
The meaning is that there is one direction because there is no distinction among its directional marks and because there is an absence of any specific mark; this being so,
it possesses oneness.
“Diversity [of direction] is due to the diversity of actions” (2.2.15).

By means of specific actions— such as the sacrificial ground for the gods being to the east and the sacrificial ground for the ancestors being to the south— the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of directions such as east, south, and so forth, arises from their diversity.
If it is argued that this involves mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), then in that case, [the definition of direction would be as follows]:
"The eastern direction is [defined] from the past, future, and present conjunction with the sun" (Pāṇini 2.2.16).

The designation "east" (*prācī*) is applied because of a non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*); that is, it is so called because it is the region of space with which the sun has conjoined, is conjoining, or will conjoin at the beginning of the day, since it faces toward the sun (*prāñcaty ādityam*).
[19,i] "In the same way, [the directions are designated as] south, west, and north. (2.2.17)
[19,ii] It is precisely from this conjunction with the sun that the designations "southern" and so forth arise.
“By this, the other directions are explained” (2.2.18).
In this very manner, the other directions— such as the southeast and so forth— are explained.

[19,v] Now, in this context, the self is to be apprehended by means of the instruments of cognition, and the instruments are [to be distinguished] from the qualities such as sound and so forth. But is it not the case that the "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) of sound and the rest is unestablished? This is said assuming that it is established. But why is there doubt regarding their being qualities? He says: Is even doubt possessed of a cause? Indeed it is. What is the cause? To this he says:
"Doubt arises from the perception of a common feature, the non-perception of specific features, and the recollection of specific features" (NS 2.2.19).

[19, vi] Perceiving the commonality of verticality in both a post and a person, yet not perceiving the specific causes such as hands or hollows, and recollecting their specific features, one consequently experiences doubt: "Is this a post, or is it not a person?
It is of two kinds: external and internal. The external is also of two kinds: perceptible and imperceptible. Regarding the imperceptible first: "The seen and the unseen" (2.2.20).
[19.viii]
When it is said that "a human being has been attained," one has doubt based on mere hearing as to whether one might see what has already been seen or what has not yet been seen;
but in the case of direct perception—
“And the seen as having been seen” (2.2.21).
[19,x] Now, for one who, having seen a person, reflects upon that very thing seen, there arises a doubt: "Has this been seen by me before, or has it not been seen?"
“It is seen as it was seen, as not seen, and in both ways, because it is seen in both ways. (2.2.22)

At first, Devadatta was seen with hair; in the middle stage, he was shaven-headed; and in the third stage, he was again with hair. In the fourth stage, through conversation and other means, and by the mere perception of his form at dawn and so forth, there arises the doubt: "Could this man be the one with hair, or perhaps the shaven-headed one? In the previous sūtra, doubt arose from the recollection of multiple objects; here, however, it arises from the recollection of specific details regarding a single object. As for the internal [doubt]:
“And from knowledge and ignorance, doubt arises” (2.2.23).

Knowledge (*vidyā*) is correct cognition; ignorance (*avidyā*) is false cognition. A fortune-teller predicted one thing auspiciously, which turned out to be true, and a second thing, which was untrue. In the third instance, there is doubt: is it true like the first state, or is it untrue like the second state? Thus has doubt been described.
[20,v] In that regard, let sound itself first be described:
"That object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing is sound" (Pāṇini 2.2.24).

That object which is apprehended by the sense of hearing is sound (*śabda*). Since the term "object" (*artha*) is not conventionally applied to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, the inclusion of the word "object" is intended to prevent the universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) from being considered sound itself.
[21,i] "In regard to that [sound], there arises the doubt: Is it a substance, an action, or a quality? (2.2.25).
[21,ii] Because it possesses a common form, there is doubt as to whether sound is a substance or something else.
Thus he says:
“Because a particularity is observed in two ways—among things of the same class and among things that are different entities.

The nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*) is observed as a specific quality of earth that distinguishes it from its own class, such as water, and from those of different classes, namely qualities and actions. Therefore, regarding sound as well, there arises a doubt: is this property of being perceivable by the auditory organ a specific quality of sound—which is equal to other qualities—or is it something distinct from them?
This is not so.
“Because it possesses a single substance, sound is not a substance” (2.2.27).

Since this sound exists in a single substance, namely space (*ākāśa*), it is not a substance; for a substance is either a non-substantial atom (*paramāṇu*) or a multi-substantial object such as a jar.
[21,vii] “Because it is not visible, action does not exist.

Whatever substance or action is perceptible by another sense faculty is also seen to be visible to the eye; however, this sound, although perceptible by the ear, is not visible to the eye. Such is the established nature of a quality (*guṇa*).
But, [21,ix] however—
“Even for that which exists as a quality (*guṇa*), there is cessation through actions; it shares the same nature as actions.

(2.2.29) [21,x] For this [sound], even though it has become a quality, there is cessation—that is, destruction—through actions, sharing the same nature as them; its destruction is inferred because it is not perceived immediately after its production.
If it is argued that there is a non-apprehension of the sign even though it exists, we say no, because of the absence of a mark for its existence. (2.2.30)

[22,ii] That which, though existent, is not apprehended due to its lack of a perceptible sign (*nimitta*), for that there exists a mark (*liṅga*) that establishes its existence; however, in the case of sound, since no mark such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) exists after it has been uttered, its non-existence is certain.
Furthermore:
"Because of the dissimilarity with that which is eternal" (2.2.31).
The destruction of what has been uttered possesses the property of being dissimilar to eternal things; therefore, it is non-eternal.
Furthermore:
“Because it is an effect.
(2.2.32) [22, vi] And sound is an effect, because it arises from conjunction and other such causes; therefore, it is non-eternal.
Furthermore: "Because of non-existence" (2.2.33).
The meaning is "due to prior non-existence. It is because of the destruction of that which possesses prior non-existence; and its prior non-existence is due to its arising from causes.
Nor are those [articulations] manifestors [of the word-sound]; why?
"Because of modification according to the cause" (2.2.34).
Because a modification of sound is perceived from causes such as a drum— [the sound being] great when the drum is large and small when it is small;
whereas, in the case of manifestation, [this would not occur].
“Because of a defect.

(2.2.35) [22,xii] If sound were manifested as something eternal, it could not be used by one person at a sacrifice and by another elsewhere, because of defects such as being exhausted (*yātayāmatva*), just like *darbha* grass and the like. Therefore, it is non-eternal.
[23,i] From what does its being an effect follow? To this he says:
“Because sound is produced from conjunction, from disjunction, and from sound. (2.2.36)

ii] Because sound is produced from the contact of a drum and a stick, from the separation of cloth and its parts, and from [another] sound— just like the succession of waves— we consider that sound is an effect. [23, iii]
“And because of an indicative mark, it is non-eternal.
(2.2.37) [23, iv] Because of the Vedic indicative mark found in the statement, “From them the three Vedas were born,” it is non-eternal.
[23,v] But is not sound eternal?
For it has been stated: "Because of the absence of two occurrences" (2.2.38).

[23, vi] For produced entities, there are two modes of activity: one is their manifestation, and the other consists in the application of their effects. The activity of a word, however—known as its utterance—is solely for the purpose of conveying meaning; it is not for its own sake. Therefore, it is eternal.
“Because of the existence of number.

(2.2.39) [23, viii] If sound were to perish as soon as it is uttered, then because it would have vanished, there could be no repetition of number in the case where "this has been recited twice"; yet such repetition does exist, therefore sound is eternal.
[23,ix] “From the word *prathama*. (Pāṇini 2.2.40) [23,x]

Regarding the phrase "from the word *prathamā*": this refers to the statement, "He recites the first verse three times" (*triḥ prathamām anvāha*). If sound were to perish as soon as it is uttered, there could be no counting of repetitions for the first *ṛc*; yet such counting does exist. Therefore, sound is eternal. [23,xi] "And because of common recognition" (2.2.41).
If sound were subject to destruction, there would be no recognition— such as the consensus that "this is that very same word 'go'"— therefore, it is eternal.
This is not the core point: "When there is multiplicity, they remain doubtful" (2.2.42).

In the case of lamps and the like, non-dual occurrence is observed; in the case of lightning, there is an absence of the number "two" as in the expression "lightning has issued forth twice"; and in the case of flames and so forth, there is consensus. Therefore, because these reasons exist even among impermanent things, they are all rendered doubtful. Consequently, [sound] is impermanent.
[24, iii] “The absence of number is general. (2.2.43)
[24,iv] The first sound and the state of common understanding— these two should be seen as similar.
<Thus ends the second chapter.>
[The First Daily Lesson of the Third Chapter] [25,i] Having thus stated the dissimilarities of the ends of the directions, he now introduces the self (ātman):
“The objects of the senses are well-known.
(3.1.1) Since sound and the other [objects] are well-known to have the nature of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, and from them the sense organs [arise], therefore now—
“The well-known existence of the senses and their objects is the reason for their being distinct from the senses and the objects.

(3.1.2) By this well-known existence of the objects to be grasped— namely, sound and so forth— which establishes the instruments such as the ear, one infers the self (*ātman*) as the cognizer who stands beyond these objects and the acts of grasping them, which are the senses and their objects.
[25,iv] “That is not a valid reason.
The reason stated for the existence of a cognizer—the one called "the establishment of the grasped and the grasping"—is unproven; that is to say, it is not a valid cause.
What is the use of such a conceptualization? Why are the sense faculties not themselves the graspers? This is not so.
“Because of the ignorance of the cause.
(3.1.4) Since the elements, which are the causes of the sense organs, are insentient, the sense organs, which are their effects, are also insentient.
[25.viii] Ignorance regarding the primary elements (*bhūta*)—
“because of ignorance regarding their effects” (3.1.5).
[25,ix] Since other effects of the primary elements, such as pots and the like, are insentient, the primary elements themselves are also insentient.
“And because of ignorance.
(3.1.6) This sūtra is intended as a summary, showing that because the elements are ignorant, the sense organs are also ignorant.
[25,xii] “That which is a different cause is not a valid reason.

The meaning is that it is something other than the characteristic of a logical reason (*hetu*); for instance, the establishment of sense-faculties and their objects would not lead to the inference of the self (*ātman*), because, being properties of the sense-faculties and objects, they lack a connection with it; therefore, it is not a valid indicator (*anapadeśa*).
This is not so.

“Conjoined, inherent, inherent in the same object, and contradictory. An effect [is a mark] of another effect; a cause [is a mark] of another cause. A non-existent contradictory [is a mark] of an existent; an existent [is a mark] of a non-existent; a non-existent [is a mark] of a non-existent; and an existent [is a mark] of an existent. (3.1.8) [26,ii]

Smoke is a conjunct mark of fire; a horn is an inherent mark of a cow. That which is inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyi*) is of two kinds: an effect [marking] another effect, as color [marks] touch; and a cause [marking] another cause, as the hand [marks] the foot. The contradictory mark (*virodhi*) is fourfold: the non-existent act of raining is the mark of the existent conjunction of wind and cloud; the existent act of raining is the mark of the non-existent conjunction of wind and cloud; the non-existent blackness is the mark of the non-existent conjunction with fire; and an existent effect is the mark of an existent conjunction with a cause. Therefore, in this case, the instrumentality and objectivity of the well-known sense organs and their objects are inherent marks of the self. If it is argued that these are not inherent in the self, this is true; however, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the sense organs must have an agent who employs them, because they are instruments, like an axe or similar tools.
[26,iii] He explains how conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the other relations can indeed serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*):
"Because a formal indicator (*apadeśa*) is preceded by what is already well-known. (3.1.9)

[26.iv] That which is well-known as a correlate (*saṃyogin*) and so forth, when it is known together with something else that is not unrelated to it, is an indicator (*liṅga*) even for that other object because of its relatedness; it is not [an indicator] if it is unrelated.
For it is said: "That which is unestablished is not a valid reason" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.10).

The contradictory (*viruddha*) is unestablished; it has no connection whatsoever with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), but rather with its opposite. This is the non-indicative (*anapadeśa*), i.e., the non-reason (*ahetu*). [27,i] “That which is non-existent and that which is doubtful are non-indicative” (NS 3.1.11).

[27,ii] That which does not exist in the subject (*pakṣa*) is, by implication, non-existent; thus the meaning is that it is "unestablished" (*asiddha*). Furthermore, "the uncertain is not a valid indicator" (*sandigdhaścānapadeśaḥ*); the meaning is that the "uncertain" (*sandigdha*) is the "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). [27,iii]
He states an example:
"‘Therefore it has horns, thus it is a horse; therefore it has horns, thus it is a cow. (3.1.12) [27, iv]

When "this object is a horse" is the probandum (*sādhya*), "having horns" (*viṣāṇitva*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because having horns is pervaded by the opposite of being a horse. When "this object is a cow" is the probandum, "having horns" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is pervaded by both the probandum and its opposite. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include what has not been explicitly stated: when "the hare has horns" is the probandum, "having horns" is unestablished (*asiddha*), because it does not reside in the subject (*pakṣa*). This was stated incidentally. Furthermore, [27,v]...
“That which is produced from the contact of the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object is distinct [from them].

(3.1.13) [27, vi] That effect called cognition, which arises from the contact of these four, exists as something distinct; there is another cause that makes the self known. Cognition requires an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) because it is an effect, just like a jar.
[27,vii] "And the occurrence and cessation [of activity] in the internal self are the mark [of its existence] in another.

The term "inner self" (*pratyagātman*) refers to the body. Activity and cessation of activity are observed in the body, and these lead to the inference of a self. The body is presided over by one possessing effort, because it possesses engagement in what is beneficial and disengagement from what is harmful, like a pot. [End of the First Daily Lesson of the Third Chapter] [Beginning of the Second Daily Lesson of the Third Chapter]
[28,i] It has been stated that the contact between the self, the sense organs, the objects, and the mind is the cause of cognition. To establish this, he states the following regarding the mind:
“The non-existence and existence of cognition when there is contact between the self, the sense organs, and the objects is the mark of the mind. (3.2.1)

[28, ii] That which, due to its absence, knowledge does not arise when there is contact between the self, the sense organs, and their objects, and which, upon its presence, knowledge arises—that is the mind (*manas*). Thus, the arising and non-arising of knowledge are the inferential marks (*liṅga*) of the mind. Its qualities (*guṇa*) are number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
“Substantiality and eternity are explained by [the case of] air” (3.2.2).
Just as the atom of air possesses substantiality and eternity because it lacks constituent parts (*adravyavattvāt*), so too does the mind.
“Because effort is not simultaneous and because cognitions are not simultaneous, the mind is one. (3.2.3)

Since multiple efforts or cognitions do not arise simultaneously with respect to many objects, it follows from the non-simultaneity of effort and cognition that there is a single mind (*manas*) in each body, which is corporeal, intangible, partless, eternal, atomic, and mobile.

[28.vii] “Inhalation, exhalation, opening and closing of the eyes, life, movement of the mind, modifications of the other sense organs, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, and effort—these are the marks (*liṅga*) of the self (*ātman*). (3.2.4)

[28, viii] The eightfold path of the noble ones (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). It consists of: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. These are called the eight factors of the noble path. They are also called the limbs of the noble path. What is right view? It is the wisdom that is the outflow of hearing and reflection, as well as the supramundane wisdom that is the outflow of cultivation, which possesses the nature of discernment regarding phenomena. This is called right view. What is right intention? It is the mental orientation that is the outflow of hearing and reflection, as well as the supramundane mental orientation that is the outflow of cultivation, which possesses the nature of directing the mind toward renunciation, non-ill will, and harmlessness. This is called right intention. What is right speech? It is the verbal expression that is the outflow of hearing and reflection, as well as the supramundane verbal expression that is the outflow of cultivation, which possesses the nature of abstaining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter. This is called right speech. What is right action? It is the bodily conduct that is the outflow of hearing and reflection, as well as the supramundane bodily conduct that is the outflow of cultivation, which possesses the nature of abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. This is called right action. What is right livelihood? It is the mode of life that is the outflow of hearing and reflection, as well as the supramundane mode of life that is the outflow of cultivation, which possesses the nature of abstaining from wrong livelihood. This is called right livelihood. What is right effort? It is the vigor that is the outflow of hearing and reflection, as well as the supramundane vigor that is the outflow of cultivation, which possesses the nature of striving for the abandonment of unwholesome states and the cultivation of wholesome states. This is called right effort. What is right mindfulness? It is the mindfulness that is the outflow of hearing and reflection, as well as the supramundane mindfulness that is the outflow of cultivation, which possesses the nature of clearly recollecting and not forgetting. This is called right mindfulness. What is right concentration? It is the one-pointedness of mind that is the outflow of hearing and reflection, as well as the supramundane one-pointedness of mind that is the outflow of cultivation, which possesses the nature of being undistracted. This is called right concentration. These are called the eight factors of the noble path. Furthermore, these eight factors of the noble path are subsumed under three categories: namely, the category of morality, the category of concentration, and the category of wisdom. Among these, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are subsumed under the category of morality; right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration are subsumed under the category of concentration; and right view and right intention are subsumed under the category of wisdom. Why is this so? Because right view is the precursor to all wholesome dharmas. Just as when a king sets out on a journey, he first dispatches a messenger ahead to clear the way, so too, when a practitioner of the path sets out on the journey of the path, right view is the precursor. Furthermore, because right view is the basis for all wholesome dharmas, it is like the earth, which is the support for all plants and trees. Furthermore, because right view is the precursor to all wholesome dharmas, it is like the rising sun, which precedes all other luminaries. Furthermore, because right view is the basis for all wholesome dharmas, it is like a great physician who is the basis for all medicinal herbs. Furthermore, because right view is the precursor to all wholesome dharmas, it is like a great king who is the precursor to his retinue. Furthermore, because right view is the basis for all wholesome dharmas, it is like a great minister who is the basis for the common people. Furthermore, because right view is the precursor to all wholesome dharmas, it is like a great leader who is the precursor to those following him. Furthermore, because right view is the basis for all wholesome dharmas, it is like a great teacher who is the basis for his disciples. Furthermore, because right view is the precursor to all wholesome dharmas, it is like a great guide who is the precursor to those traveling with him. Furthermore, because right view is the basis for all wholesome dharmas, it is like a great architect who is the basis for the construction of a house. Furthermore, because right view is the precursor to all wholesome dharmas, it is like a great pilot who is the precursor to those crossing the sea. Furthermore, because right view is the basis for all wholesome dharmas, it is like a great shipowner who is the basis for the merchants. Inhalation and exhalation (*prāṇāpāna*), the opening and closing of the eyes (*nimeṣonmeṣa*), and the movement of the mind (*manogati*) are signs of the self (*ātman*) because they are produced by effort; life (*jīvana*) is a sign because it is an effect of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); the modifications of other sense organs are signs because they arise from memory; and pleasure and so forth are signs because they are qualities [belonging to a substance]. The activity of inhalation and exhalation belonging to the air (*vāyu*) residing within the body is produced by effort, because—while having as its object the air contained within the body—it is a modified state, like the movement of air contained within a bellows. The action of the opening and closing of the eyes is also produced by effort, because it is denoted by the term "action of opening and closing the eyes," like the action of opening and closing a wooden mechanical doll. The conjunction of the self with the mind, which depends on the unseen force, is life; the growth of the body and so forth are also effects of that [life], and thus constitute life. The body is presided over by one possessing effort, because it is the cause of growth, decay, fracture, and healing, like an old house [being maintained]. The movement of the mind toward another sense organ is produced by effort, because it has as its cause a connection with a desired location, like the movement of a ball; for that [movement] is produced by the effort of a child. The production of the perception of color, the manifestation of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the recollection of taste, effort, the action of the mind, the connection between the tongue and the mind, and the modification of the tongue occurs because each preceding factor is the cause of each subsequent one. However, their cognition occurs in the reverse order: the self is inferred through the recollection of each preceding factor from each subsequent one. Memory does not belong to the sense organs, because what was seen by one cannot be remembered by another. Nor does it belong to a part of the body, because [the body] changes according to different states. Uddyotakara [states in *Nyāyavārttika* 1.1.10]: "Devadatta’s cognitions of color, taste, smell, and touch have a single [underlying] cause, because they are synthesized by the cognition ‘by me,’ just as many people who have made an agreement simultaneously perceive many things when a dancer raises her eyebrows."
[28,ix] Furthermore, pleasure and the other qualities depend upon a substratum possessing those qualities, because they are qualities, like color.
“Substantiality and eternity are explained by [the case of] air.
(3.2.5) [28,xi] Because it lacks constituent parts (*adravyavattvāt*), its substantiality and eternity are like those of atoms and air.
[28,xii] But is it not the case that, regarding the statement, "In the case of 'Yajñadatta,' because there is no perception despite proximity, no observed mark (*liṅga*) exists" (3.2.6)?

[28,xiii] Just as when there is contact with an object of sight, there arises the perceptual cognition "this is Yajñadatta," it is not so that a cognition arises such as "this Self is connected to breath and so forth, or to pleasure and so forth. Now, how can breath and so forth, whose connection [to the Self] has not been perceived, be a mark (*liṅga*) of the Self? To this he says: "Breath and so forth are not a perceived mark.
“And there is no distinction [from the inference based on general observation].

(3.2.7) [28,xv] Since breath and the like do not arise without a cause, and pleasure and the like do not exist without a substratum, these must have some cause and substratum; therefore, because even this inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) does not exclude ether and the other [elements], there is no distinction, as it is possible for those too to be the cause.
“Therefore, it is based on scripture. (3.2.8) [28,xvii]
The meaning is that the claim "the self exists" is a mere conventional expression;
this is not so.
“Because it is distinct from the word ‘I,’ it is not derived from scripture.

(3.2.9) [28,xix] Because there is grammatical coreferentiality (*aikādhikaraṇya*) with the word ‘I’— which has as its object a substance of the self (*ātman*) distinct from earth and the other elements— as in “I possess breath and so forth,” or “I possess happiness,” it is therefore not derived from scripture, since it is based on the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of breath and the like.
[30,i] But is it not the case that: “And if [one thinks], ‘I am Devadatta,’ or ‘I am Yajñadatta,’ [this is] what is directly perceived”? (3.2.10)

[30, ii] If indeed this were a perceptible observation regarding the self, such as "I am Devadatta" or "I am Yajñadatta," then it would be appropriate to maintain that the word "I" denotes the self; however, since the word "I" shares the same referential locus as the word "Devadatta"—which denotes the body—the word "I" also denotes the body. Therefore, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth, are not grounds for determining the existence of a self.
He explains how the word "Devadatta" applies to the body:
"The perception of the body as 'Devadatta goes' or 'Viṣṇumitra goes' occurs through metaphorical designation" (3.2.11).

Because it is used together with the word "goes" (*gacchati*), which denotes motion, the word "Devadatta" is determined to refer to the body, since motion is impossible for the self (*ātman*). Therefore, the word "I" (*aham*) also refers only to the body, because it is observed to be used together with the word "Devadatta.
This is not so.
"But the metaphorical usage is doubtful" (3.2.12).

Because the word "Devadatta" shares a common substratum with a single object, this metaphorical application of the word "I" to the body is doubtful: is the word "I" used metaphorically as denoting the self because the body assists the self, or is it primarily denotative of the body itself? Thus, there is no certainty regarding whether the word "I" refers to the body or the self.

[30,vii] He states the certainty regarding his own position: “Because it exists in relation to the inner self as ‘I’ and because it does not exist in relation to external objects, it is a perception of something distinct. (3.2.13)

"In the inner self" means in the *ātman*; "in the other" means in the body. If the word "I" (*aham*) were denotative of the body, then it would be used by everyone with respect to that physical mass, just as the word "Devadatta" is; but this is not the case. Therefore, the word "I" is directly perceived as referring to the inner self, which is a distinct entity.

If it is argued that, as with the body, there could likewise be no [difference] in the self because of the application of qualities by others, he says in response: “But there is no difference in knowledge between Yajñadatta and Viṣṇumitra due to a difference in their bodies. (3.2.14)

Just as, from the observation of the specific bodies belonging to Yajñadatta and Viṣṇumitra, knowledge of their pleasure and so forth does not arise in people like us, in the same way, their "I-consciousness" (ahaṅkāra) is not perceived by us such that the word "I" could be applied to it. If, however, [the word "I"] denoted the body, then just as people apply the word "Devadatta" to the body upon seeing it, they would likewise apply this [word "I"] to it; but they do not do so. Therefore, it does not reside in the body. If, on the other hand, it resides in the self (ātman), its non-application by others follows. Thus, because they share the same substratum with the word "I," pleasure and so forth have the self as their object, and the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth are caused by that [self].
[31,i] But is it not the case that "there is a single self because there is no distinction in the production of pleasure, pain, and cognition" (3.2.15)?

[31,ii] Just as there is a single existence because there is no distinction in the general mark and an absence of a specific mark, so too there is a single self-nature because there is no distinction in the production of pleasure, pain, and cognition, and an absence of a specific mark.
This is not so,
because they are established as distinct [entities].
Because one person possesses happiness and so forth while another lacks them, the selves are multiple according to this arrangement;
[this is established] "by the authority of the scripture" (3.2.17).

[31, vi] From the authority of such scriptural injunctions as "One who desires a village should sacrifice" and "One who desires heaven should sacrifice," it follows that there are many selves (*ātman*). Its specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*) are intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Other qualities, however, are number (*saṃkhyā*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and disjunction (*vibhāga*). <|| Third Chapter ||>
[First Āhnika of the Fourth Chapter] Having thus described the substances, he now discusses their permanence, perception, and non-perception, as well as other matters incidentally.
“Whatever exists that is without a cause is eternal” (4.1.1).
By the phrase “because it does not consist of substance,” it is stated that whatever exists without a cause— such as atoms and so forth— is eternal.
But regarding perception, "its effect is the mark" (4.1.2).
[32.iv] Although that [entity], such as an atom and so forth, is not perceived by the sense organs, its effect— such as the body or the great elements— is its inferential mark. [32.v]
For it is said: "The existence of the effect indeed follows from the existence of the cause" (4.1.3).
Since an effect, such as a cloth, arises from causes such as threads, the effect is the mark (liṅga) of the cause because the effect is preceded by its cause.
Furthermore, the statement "it is impermanent" constitutes a negation of a specific [quality]. (4.1.4)
[32.viii] When it is indeed stated that "all effects are impermanent," then by this specific negation of permanence regarding the domain of effects, it is understood that some cause is permanent.
“And ignorance.

(4.1.5) Ignorance is the non-apprehension of atoms due to their being beyond the senses; that too precludes impermanence. For when an object is not perceived, by whom could its impermanence be apprehended? Therefore, impermanence cannot be asserted.
If it is asked how perception occurs, [the answer is]:
“Perception arises from magnitude, from the possession of multiple substances, and from color. (4.1.6)

[33,ii] With respect to a substance in which the dimension of magnitude (mahattva-parimāṇa) inheres, cognition arises from both the plurality of the substances that are its inherent causes and from qualities such as white color.
Whence is this? Because:
"Due to the absence of constituent substances, there is no perception of the atom" (4.1.7).
Even though color exists, there is no perception of an atom because of the absence of a substance as its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
[33,v] "Or, due to the absence of the formation of color, there is no perception of air" (4.1.8).

[33, vi] Even though it possesses multiple constituent substances and magnitude, there is no perception of air due to the absence of the conditioning factor known as color (*rūpa*). Because the specific quality of possessing multiple constituent substances must be apprehended, the non-perception of even a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is established.
Regarding color-form (*rūpa*), how is it perceived?
“Perception occurs through inherence in a substance composed of multiple substances, and due to the specific nature of the color-form itself.

The perception of color occurs through its inherence in a large substance composed of many constituent parts, such as a jar, and through the particularity of color itself, which is a specific universal known as *rūpatva*.
[33, ix] "By this, the cognition of taste, smell, and touch is explained. (4.1.10)

[33,x] By this aforementioned principle, the perception of tastes and so forth occurs through inherence in a substance composed of multiple substances, and from the specific universals such as "tasteness" (*rasatva*) and so on.
“Because of the absence of that, there is no deviation.

(4.1.11) [33,xii] Since the form of an atom does not exist through inherence (*samavāya*) in a substance composed of multiple substances, it is not perceived; therefore, there is no deviation between the perception of form and its inherence in a substance composed of multiple substances.

[33,xiii] “Numbers, dimensions, distinctness, conjunction and disjunction, priority and posteriority, and action are perceptible by the eye because they inhere in substances possessing color. (4.1.12) [33,xiv]

"Material" (*rūpin*) means possessing a specific form; because they are inherent in that material thing which is capable of being perceived, these [substances] are visible, as are their own specific universals (*svasāmānyaviśeṣa*).
Why? [34,i]
“Because they are invisible among formless things. (4.1.13) Since those [qualities] situated in other large substances that are devoid of color-and-shape (rūpa) are not perceived.
[34,iii] “By this, sensory cognition regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and substances (*bhāva*) is explained.

Just as there is perception of color and other qualities that are inherent in a large substance due to their inherence in it, so too, when qualities are inherent in a large [substance], there is the perception of the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and existence (*bhāva*) inherent in those qualities by means of the respective sense organs, such as the eye, due to their inherence in those various qualities like color and the rest; however, the generalities and particularities (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) are not the perceivers of them, because they are absent [therein]. Likewise, [the perception of] substantiality (*tattva*) and so forth occurs through their own respective sense organs; but in the case of a substance, it is due to the inherence of existence (*bhāva*). In the case of action (*karman*), it is due to inherence in that which is inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), just as in the case of a quality. [End of the First Daily Lesson of the Fourth Book]
[The Second Section of the Fourth Chapter] [35,i] Now, their internal function is stated; therein—
“Because the conjunction of perceptible and imperceptible [substances] is itself imperceptible, the body composed of five elements does not exist.

(4.2.1) [35, ii] Since three of the five elements beginning with earth are perceptible while air is imperceptible, just as their conjunction with that [imperceptible element] is likewise imperceptible, so too the body would be imperceptible, because it is composed of both perceptible and imperceptible [elements]. However, because it is indeed perceptible, we conclude that it is not composed of all five [elements].
[35,iii] But would it not rather be composed of three [qualities], since it is said: “And because no other quality appears, it does not consist of three natures either”? (4.2.2)

[35.iv] If, at the commencement [of creation], by means of earth, water, and fire, distinct forms and other qualities were to arise as effects from heterogeneous forms and so forth, it would not be so; rather, we perceive only those forms and other qualities that belong to the earth. Therefore, [the world] is not composed of three elements.

“But the mutual conjunction of the five with the self is not prohibited. (4.2.3) [35, vi] By the word *ātman*, one’s own nature (*svarūpa*) is meant; by way of their own nature, the mutual conjunction of all five elements is not prohibited in the body as non-producers [of further effects]. In an earthly body, water and the other elements are conjoined, but not inherent (*samavāyin*). In Varuṇa’s world and elsewhere, a body is produced from water and the other elements that is indeed non-uterine (*ayonija*).
Why?
"Because it is preceded by many locations. (4.2.4)
[35, viii] Atoms have multiple spatial parts; by these alone is the body of water and so forth produced, and not from semen and blood.
And that [is known] "from the specific nature of the property" (4.2.5).
Only atoms that depend upon specific dharmas initiate a body, not semen and the like. For how could the bodies of those possessing merit consist of semen and such?
Furthermore:
“Because of a specific effect” (4.2.6).
From a specific effect known as the bodies of locusts and the like, we conclude that there exist beings not born from a womb.
[36,iii] For this reason as well: "Because of the absence of a designation" (4.2.7).
iv] Because there are designations such as "born from coals" (*aṅgārebhyo jātaḥ*) and "made of coals" (*aṅgitāḥ*), we consider that there are beings not born from a womb (*ayonija*).
Why?
"Because it possesses ideation and so forth" (4.2.8).

Since names such as "Aṅgirā" and so forth are applied by those who have perceived through direct perception objects such as the birth of Aṅgiras, the designations are consistent with reality because names possess a beginning.
Therefore:
“There are those not born from a womb, on account of an indicative mark in the Veda.

(4.2.9) [36, viii] From such an indicative mark in the Veda as “The moon was born from the mind,” there exist specific bodies that are not born from a womb. Thus, bodies composed of water and so forth are exclusively non-uterine; however, earthy bodies are both uterine and non-uterine.

Having thus stated the qualities without omitting any, he now describes the actions therein, since they are few in number:
"Action in the hand arises from its conjunction with the self and from effort" (5.1.1).

Since effort depends upon conjunction with its own substratum for the initiation of action, the conjunction between the self and the hand is the cause of the motion. Because conjunction is a dependent cause, effort is also a cause. Therefore, the motion in the hand arises from both.
Likewise, the motion of the pestle arises from the conjunction with the hand. (5.1.2)

[37,iv] "In the same way" means that only the number is extended by analogy; therefore, the conjunction between the hand and the pestle is the cause of the action of the pestle, as is the previously mentioned effort. However, the conjunction between the self and the hand is not the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the action of the pestle, because that [action] is established solely from the conjunction of the hand with the self-conjoined [hand].

“In the case of the action of a pestle produced by impact, the conjunction with the hand is not the cause because of its absence. (5.1.3) [37, vi] Impact is the conjunction with a substance possessing velocity (*vega*). In the action of upward-leaping produced in the pestle by the impact of the mortar, the conjunction between the hand and the pestle is not the cause; for the previous effort has been destroyed by the impact, and since there is no desire such as “let the pestle-substance leap up,” there is an absence of any further effort. Furthermore, since conjunction is a dependent cause in the initiation of qualities and actions, a conjunction between the hand and the pestle devoid of effort is not the cause of the leaping.
[37,vii] “Likewise, there is the conjunction of the self in the action of the hand and the pestle. (5.1.4) [37,viii]

Just as the conjunction of the hand and the pestle is not the cause for the action of the pestle’s upward flight, so too the conjunction of the self and the hand is not the cause for the action of the hand’s upward flight, because conjunction is a dependent cause; this is due to the absence of an intention such as "let the hand fly up together with the pestle" and the absence of volitional effort (*prayatna*).
If it is asked, "Whence then comes the upward flight of those two? [the answer follows].

“From the impact of the pestle—that is, from the conjunction with the pestle—there is action in the hand. (5.1.5) [37,x] The impact against the mortar is the cause of the upward-flying action of the pestle; however, the conjunction between the hand and the pestle, depending on the velocity inherent in the pestle, is the cause of the action in the hand, whereas the impact itself is not, because it does not reside in the same substrate as the action.
[38,i] “Likewise, from the conjunction of the self, the hand, and the action. (5.1.6) [38,ii]

"Ātman" refers to a single part of the body; just as there is non-cognitive action in both the hand and the mace, so too, at the time of the hand's upward movement, due to the conjunction with a part of the hand and depending on the velocity residing in the hand, non-cognitive action arises in that very part.
[38, iii] "In the absence of conjunction, falling occurs due to gravity. (5.1.7)
[38,iv] When the conjunction between the hand and the club has ceased due to disjunction, falling occurs because of gravity.

“Because there is no specific impulsion (*nodana*), there is no upward or horizontal motion. (5.1.8) [38, vi] That by which something is impelled is *nodana*; it is a specific kind of contact dependent upon velocity and effort. In the absence of the effort of the impeller, there is an absence of impulsion; therefore, due to gravity alone, there is no action of motion—neither upward nor horizontally—in such things as a pestle.
[38,vii] From what does the particularity of the impulse arise?
“The particularity of the impulse arises from a particularity of effort. (5.1.9)

viii] Here, the effort produced by a specific desire, such as "I shall throw this here," generates a conjunction between a substance such as the hand and another substance, which is termed "impulsion" (nodana).
“From a particular impulsion comes a particular projection” (5.1.10).
A particular impulsion, produced from an effort characterized by the desire to propel an object to a distant place, effects its casting to that distant location.
[38,xi] “By means of manual labor, the work of a child is explained. (5.1.11) [38,xii]

The action of the embryo, such as its throbbing and so forth, occurs with a cause (*sapratyaya*), arising from the conjunction of the self and the body in dependence upon an effort preceded by life. The action of the embryo approaching the mother’s place of excrement is without a cause (*apratyaya*), arising from the conjunction of the self and the body in dependence upon the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Likewise, the bursting of a blister on one who has been burned [is without a cause]. (5.1.12)

[38,xiv] As for the throwing of a burning object from the hand while the mind is distracted, that too arises from the conjunction of the self and the hand, which depends upon an effort preceded by life; thus, it is not without a cause.
“In the absence of effort, there is falling of one who is asleep due to gravity.
(5.1.13) [38,xvi] In the absence of the effort that sustains the body, the limbs of one who is asleep fall because of gravity, since at that time there is an absence of volition.
[39,i] “The action of grass arises from conjunction with the wind.
The motion of grass and other such things arises from the conjunction of wind and grass, which depends upon momentum (*vega*), because they lack effort (*prayatna*).
[39, iii] "The movement of a gem and the gliding of a needle are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). (5.1.15)
The meaning is that the movement of jewels toward a thief and of needles toward a magnet is produced by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).

“Specific conjunctions occurring non-simultaneously are the cause for the diversity of actions in an arrow” (5.1.16). Due to the initial impulse (*nodana*), the first action arises; due to the resulting momentum (*saṃskāra*), many subsequent actions arise in the arrow. For if there were only a single action, that action would be destroyed by the very first conjunction with space, and consequently, no further conjunctions or disjunctions could arise from that action. Therefore, there are multiple actions in the arrow.
“From the initial impulsion of the arrow comes its first action; and from the formative force (*saṃskāra*) produced by that action, there arises a subsequent action, and likewise each succeeding one.

The conjunction of the bowstring and the arrow—whether depending on an effort or depending on the velocity of the string—is the impulsion (*nodana*). From that, the first action of the arrow produces a momentum (*saṃskāra*) dependent on the impulsion; however, independent of it, it produces conjunctions and disjunctions. Then, when the action has ceased due to the conjunction and the impulsion has ceased due to the disjunction, the momentum born from the first action produces a subsequent action in the arrow; likewise, each subsequent action follows in succession. [39,ix] “In the absence of momentum, falling occurs due to gravity. (5.1.18)
Through conjunction with a substance possessing touch, the destruction of the [impelling] disposition occurs, whereby gravity effects the action of falling.

[The Second Daily Lesson of the Fifth Chapter] [40,i] Having explained the actions pertaining to the internal [selves] and those connected to them, he now explains the actions of the great elements (mahābhūta).
“Action in earth arises from pushing, from striking, and from conjunction with that which is conjoined.

That particular kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) which, independent of gravity, fluidity, momentum, and effort, is the cause of action that results from pushing or impelling (*nodana*)—that is, from an action that causes non-separation—is *nodana*. For instance, action arises in the earth known as mud when it is pushed by feet and the like. Impact (*abhighāta*) is a conjunction dependent on momentum that is the cause of action resulting from striking—that is, an action that causes separation. For instance, action is observed in certain parts of the earth due to impact from chariots and the like. Furthermore, actions occur in objects conjoined with those being pushed or struck, through conjunction with what is already conjoined.
[40,iii] “That is produced by an unseen force through its specific distinction.

Indeed, that action such as trembling which arises throughout the entire earth due to the conjunction of air with opposing motions, produced for the purpose of indicating the auspicious or inauspicious fortune of living beings, is caused by the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) of all beings specifically because it indicates their auspicious or inauspicious fortune.
[40,v] “In the absence of conjunction with water, falling occurs due to heaviness. (5.2.3)
In the absence of the conjunction of the supporting wind and clouds, the action of falling occurs due to the heaviness of water.
"That [falling] is specifically caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). (5.2.4)
[40,vii] The action of falling, produced by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) for the sake of the prosperity or destruction of crops, is called "caused by the unseen force" (*adṛṣṭakārita*).
[40,viii]
“From fluidity comes flowing” (5.2.5).
Due to the absence of a restraining factor, the action of flowing in water arises from fluidity.
“By means of the *nāḍī*, through conjunction with the wind, there is ascent.

(5.2.6) [41, ii] The term *nāḍī* refers to a ray; the Sun has two rays—*Śuci* and *Śukra*. *Śuci* draws up the waters, while *Śukra* effects growth. By means of the *nāḍī* called *Śuci*, conjoined with the wind and depending upon the effort of the Sun, there is ascent.
“Because of non-enjoyment, because of oppression, and because of the connection of what is already connected. (5.2.7)

Climbing by means of being pushed with variegated sticks and the like, or by being pressed with clothes and the like, occurs when there is contact with both that which is being pressed and that which is being moved;
[41,v] "the climbing of trees is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). (5.2.8)
vi] It is by means of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) that water poured at the root of a tree rises up to the top of the tree.
“The solidification of water and the melting of fire result from conjunction.
(5.2.9) The solidification of water—that is, its hardness—results from conjunction with celestial fire; however, melting results from both celestial and terrestrial fire.
[41,ix] “In that case, thundering is the indicative mark.
Regarding the statement, “There is fire in divine waters,” the evidence for fire is its manifestation as lightning issuing forth from the clouds.
[41,xi] And there is Vedic authority as well: (5.2.11).
And the Vedic statement, “They have conceived that fire as a germ for adornment,” is a sign of fire within the celestial waters.
“Thunder arises from the conjunction and the disjunction of water.

(5.2.12) [41,xiv] Thunder is the sound of clouds and lightning. Sound arises from conjunction, specifically from the mutual impact of water particles that have become waves and are impelled by two winds moving in opposite directions. Sound also arises from the disjunction of water particles when they are separated by even a single turbulent wind.
“By means of the action of earth, the action of fire and the action of air have been explained. (5.2.13)

Just as action occurs in earth due to impulsion, impact, conjunction-with-conjunction, or the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), so too it occurs in fire and air. This is non-restricted action. But restricted action is as follows—
“The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of air, and the initial actions of atoms and the mind are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). (5.2.14) [42, ii]

If fire did not possess upward flaming, or if it moved only horizontally, then that which is being cooked would either fail to become ash or would instead turn into water. Likewise, if air did not move horizontally, there would be no fanning of substances being purified, and fire would lack its awakening. Furthermore, at the beginning of a creation, the initial action of mutual approach among the atoms of earth and other elements belonging to souls whose bodies have perished would not occur; similarly, for yogis who have attained mastery and, at the end of a kalpa, intentionally separate their minds from their bodies through effort so that they remain distinct, the initial action of the mind toward a new body at the start of a creation would not take place without the influence of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). Therefore, the upward flaming of fire, the horizontal blowing of air, the action of approach in atoms, and the initial action of the mind—these are produced by the unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) of living beings.
[42,iii] “By means of manual action, the action of the mind is explained. (5.2.15) [42,iv]

Just as there is action in the hand due to both its conjunction with the self and effort, so too there is action in the mind due to its conjunction with the self and effort; this is the action of one possessing a body. Among these, for one who is awake, it arises from effort preceded by desire and aversion, whereas at the time of awakening [from meditation], it arises from that preceded by the life-force (*jīvana*).
Since conjunction is *yoga* and that is the effect of action, action is therefore a limb of *yoga*; moreover, both *yoga* and liberation are discussed even within the context of action.
“From the contact of the self, the sense organs, the mind, and the objects, pleasure and pain arise; therefore, there is the non-commencement of that.

(5.2.16) [42, vi] Since the contact of the self, the sense organs, the mind, and the objects produces pleasure and pain by being the cause of cognition, "the non-commencement of that" means the non-commencement—that is, the non-arising—of that contact is stated.
For it is said: "When the mind is established in the Self, there is an absence of pleasure and pain for one who possesses a body; that is Yoga" (5.2.17).

[42.viii] For when the mind is situated in the self and not in the sense organs, then, because the fourfold contact has not been initiated, there is an absence of pleasure and pain—which are its effects. This is the yoga, consisting of the conjunction of the self with the mind, which, for the self possessing a body, depends upon the restraint of the vital breath (*vāyu*).
Why has the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), which is a limb of yoga, not been mentioned?
[It is because] "the action of the self is explained by the action of the body" (5.2.18).

In this context, by the word "self" (*ātman*), the vital air (*vāyu*) is meant; just as action occurs in the hand through the conjunction of the self and effort, so too does the action of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) arise from the conjunction of the self and the vital air, and from effort. [43, iii] "Withdrawal, movement toward, conjunction with what is eaten and drunk, and conjunctions with other effects—these are caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). (VS 5.2.19)

[43.iv] At the time of death, the departure or withdrawal of the mind from the previous body is *apasarpaṇa*; the connection of the mind with another body is *upasarpaṇa*. The connection of the embryo, from the stage of semen and blood onwards, with the food and drink consumed by the mother that enters through the channels is the "conjunction with what is eaten and drunk" (*aśitapītasaṃyoga*). Those connections within a single cycle of existence, such as the stages of the embryo (*kalala*), the bubble (*arbuda*), the lump of flesh (*peśī*), the solid mass (*ghana*), and so forth, are "conjunctions with other effects" (*kāryāntarasaṃyoga*). These, beginning with *apasarpaṇa* and the others, are brought about by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) alone, not by volitional effort (*prayatna*).
“In the absence of that, there is an absence of conjunction, which is non-manifestation; that is liberation.

(5.2.20) Thus, in the absence of *adṛṣṭa*—which has as its causes such things as beginningless wandering (*apasarpaṇa*)—there occurs the absence of the conjunction between the self and the mind known as "living," and the non-manifestation of another body; this is liberation.

Because all [perception] is obscured by darkness, when knowledge does not arise, darkness is the cause. Furthermore, that [darkness] is—“Darkness is merely the absence of existence, due to its dissimilarity to substance, quality, and action. (VS 5.2.21)

[43, viii] Darkness is not a substance, because it possesses the property of perishability and thus differs from eternal substances; and because it possesses the properties of being incorporeal, intangible, and opposed to luminosity, it differs from impermanent substances. Nor is it a quality or an action, since no substratum for such qualities or actions is perceived. Therefore, darkness is merely the absence of light.
Why is this so?
"And because light is obstructed by another substance" (5.2.22).

Because light—such as the radiance of the sun—is present externally, yet absent in places like mountain caves when covered by other substances, we consider darkness to be the mere absence of light. External darkness is dispelled by lamps and the like, whereas that which consists of ignorance is dispelled by the light of knowledge; thus have yoga and liberation been described.
[44,i] "Space, time, and ether are devoid of action because they possess properties different from those that possess action. (5.2.23)

[44,ii] Space, time, and the directions are formless; because they possess a nature dissimilar to earth and other substances which possess activity—namely, being formless—they are devoid of action. By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that the self (ātman) is also devoid of action.
“By this, actions and qualities are explained.
(5.2.24) [44, iv] By this—namely, by their incorporeality—it is established that qualities and actions are inactive substances; and by the word “and” (*ca*), universals and so forth are included.
“The conjunction of inactive things is denied on account of their actions. (5.2.25)
Action does not inhere in inactive things such as impact and the like, because it produces action in its own substratum.
[44, vii] “But the qualities that are non-inherent causes [are the cause of action]. (5.2.26)
viii] For that which has qualities as its cause, those very qualities are the non-inherent cause.
“By its qualities, direction is explained” (5.2.27).

Direction has been explained as the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for the distinction of suffixes such as “going out by the east”; this extension is on the basis of being a cause, not on the basis of being an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*).
[44,xi] “Time is by reason of its causes. (5.2.28) [44,xii]

By the very same reason through which space was explained as being the cause of the diversity of cognitions, by that same [reason] the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) for the diversity of cognitions such as "produced simultaneously" and so forth has been explained.
[Chapter Five: The Section on Action is Completed.
[The First Daily Lesson of the Sixth Chapter.]

[45,i] Having explained the actions (*karma*), the qualities (*guṇa*) are now explained. Among these, *dharma* is explained first, because it was the subject introduced at the beginning of the treatise. Its means of accomplishment is the Vedic injunction. If it is asked, "From what does the truth of the Veda derive?", it is because—"The composition of sentences in the Veda is preceded by intelligence" (6.1.1).

[45,ii] A composition such as “One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice,” which is the work of the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, is preceded by intelligence; therefore, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because being composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) is invariably concomitant with truthfulness.
If it is argued that what is beyond the senses cannot be known, [the author replies]:
“And there is no sign for the Sage [to be inferred] from our cognitions.

That by which an object is indicated (*liṅgyate*) is the "indicator" (*liṅga*), namely, cognition (*vijñāna*). For the Blessed One’s cognition is not exactly like our own cognition, which has as its object an entity that is present, unobstructed, and connected [to the senses]. Therefore, it is possible for the Blessed One to possess a cognition whose object is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya-artha*).
How is this known?

“Likewise, the accomplishment of the application of names for a Brāhmaṇa and so forth is the indicative mark. (6.1.3) [45, vi] For us, when considering an object such as a Brāhmaṇa without instruction, the cognition “this is a Brāhmaṇa” does not arise through perception. And it is observed that the formulation of names occurs after perceiving an object through perception, as in the case of a son and others. These names, such as “Brāhmaṇa” and so forth, do exist; therefore, they explain the meaning of the sūtra as follows: those names were formulated by one who has perceived the object through perception.
Therefore:
"The act of giving is preceded by an intention. (Pāṇini 6.1.4)

[45, viii] Precisely because the composition of sentences and words in the Vedas and other scriptures is the work of the Supreme Lord, this rule concerning gifts and so forth, though based on tradition (*smārta*), is the result of the deliberate intention of Bhṛgu and others who, having examined His sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) divided into infinite branches, authorized a concise summary. Thus, the rules concerning gifts and so forth are causes of *dharma*.

“Likewise, receiving gifts. (6.1.5) In the same way, even the receiving of gifts— for one whose mental fluctuations have ceased, who is born of pure descent, and who is endowed with qualities conducive to receiving— conduces solely to dharma.
[46,iii] "The sequence of these two is as follows: 'of those that do not function as mutual members' (6.1.6).

Just as entities are not mutually related as cause and effect—since the fire-drill (*araṇi*) is not the cause of fire, but rather its own constituent parts—and yet there is a sequence between the fire-drill and the fire; so too, in these two cases, first comes the act of giving and afterwards the act of receiving, but there is no relationship of cause and effect. Why? [46,v]
“Because the qualities of one self are not the cause of the qualities of another self.
(6.1.7) For indeed, the qualities of one self do not become the cause of the qualities of another self.
In this regard:
"From eating what is not faulty and from speaking in harmony, there is prosperity. (6.1.8)

[46, viii] By feeding a Brahmin who is free from fault, a person’s prosperity arises from the utterance of his benedictions and so forth; the meaning is that dharma becomes the cause of that. [46, ix]
“That is not found in the case of feeding a wicked person” (6.1.9).
Even though one utters words of benediction and the like, no prosperity is attained after having fed a wicked Brāhmaṇa.
[46,xi] Now, what is *duṣṭa*? "The root *duṣ* is used in the sense of harming" (Pāṇini 6.1.10).
Know that one who is engaged in harming another—harming being of the nature of physical or mental suffering—is wicked. The word "harming" (hiṃsā) is illustrative; for:
[46,xiii]
“There is a fault arising from association” (6.1.11).

One who has committed a great sin is joined with fault by mere conversation; how much more so by eating and the like? Here, "association" (*samabhivyāhāra*) means conversation, whereas in the previous case it meant bestowing a blessing.
“That does not exist when it is not defective. (6.1.12)
Indeed, that refutation based on co-utterance does not apply to a Brahmin who is free from violence and other such faults;
even when he is faultless— [47,i] — it does not apply.
“Activity is directed toward the distinguished.

(6.1.13) Activity for one who seeks prosperity is not directed toward anyone merely devoid of violence and so forth; rather, it is directed toward a Brāhmaṇa who is distinguished by his place, time, knowledge, and conduct.
[47,iii] Thereafter: “There is no engagement with what is equal or inferior. (6.1.14)

[47,iv] A Brāhmaṇa who is free from defects and endowed with qualities such as [proper] lineage (*deśa*) and so forth is called "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*). One endowed with even one of these qualities is "equal" (*sama*). One endowed with all of them is "distinguished. Apart from those two, another—whether he be defective, or a Kṣatriya and so forth, or even a mere living being—is called "inferior" (*hīna*). In that regard, for one desiring worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), there is no engagement in the giving of gold and other things preceded by mantras on occasions such as the Vaiśākhī festival with respect to an equal or an inferior; rather, it is with respect to a distinguished recipient. [47,v]
“By this, taking from others what belongs to those who are inferior, equal, or superior is explained.
(6.1.15) [47, vi] By this, in the reverse order, the taking of another’s property in times of distress is explained. And it has been said:
“First, one should take from a low person; in his absence, even from an equal. But if that is impossible, one may take even from a distinguished righteous person.
“Likewise, there is the abandonment of those who are hostile. (6.1.16) [47,
viii] By this very same reverse order, a Brahmin who has been challenged by inferior enemies for the purpose of being killed should go forth against those very enemies.
[47,ix] “The sacrifice of oneself or the sacrifice for others is the same.

When a Brāhmaṇa who is equal to oneself in qualities has been attacked by an enemy, there is an option: either one's own death or that of the assailant. [47.xi] "In the case of a superior [enemy], one should sacrifice oneself. (6.1.18)

[47,xii] When one has been overtaken by an enemy possessing superior qualities, one must accept even one's own death at the hands of that foe. In this context, the designation of "inferior" and so forth is made with respect to the self; however, in the case of receiving gifts, it is relative to the recipients themselves.
<Thus ends the first daily lesson of the sixth chapter.>

“Regarding those acts whose purpose is seen and which have been observed in the Śruti and Smṛti, their performance when the visible result is absent leads to spiritual prosperity. (6.2.1) [48, ii] The performance of acts such as bathing, which are prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti and have a visible purpose such as the removal of impurities, leads to spiritual prosperity when that visible result is not intended.
[48,iii] What are they?

“Consecration, fasting, celibacy, residence in the teacher’s house, forest-dwelling, sacrifice, giving, sprinkling, and the injunctions regarding direction, asterism, mantra, and time, are for the sake of the unseen. (6.2.2)

Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how is it that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as real, nor does he perceive any dharma as unreal?
