*Abhiṣecana* (ablution) is the contact of the body with water at a specific place and time; it is bathing. *Upavāsa* (fasting) consists of abstaining from food for a day and night, preceded by a formal vow. By the word *brahman*, the Self (*ātman*) is meant; *brahmacarya* (celibacy) is the union of the self and the mind directed toward the *brahman*, consisting of the avoidance of women and other such things. *Gurukulavāsa* (residence in the teacher’s house) is the dwelling in the teacher’s home by one who is intent on serving the teacher and seeks knowledge and the like. A *vānaprastha* is one who, having departed from his home according to scriptural injunction, has set out for the forest; his duty is *vānaprasthya*. *Yajñas* are sacrifices such as the *pākayajña* and others. *Dāna* (charity) is the giving of gold and the like, as well as the granting of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*). *Prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) refers to the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) and similar rites. Other specific rules include the restriction of direction (*diṅniyama*) and so forth. Regarding the restriction of direction: "One should eat food facing the east. Regarding the restriction of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*): "One should establish the sacred fires under the *Kṛttikā* constellation. Regarding the restriction of mantra: "He offers [the oblation] with the words *devasya tvā*. Regarding the restriction of time (*kāla*): "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in the spring. Thus, all this, when performed while setting aside any visible motive, conduces to *dharma*.
In this regard:
“The four stages of life [are derived from the root *āśram*] by means of both the presence and the absence of the suffix *upa*. (Pāṇini 6.2.3)
[48, vi] This refers to the activity of the four types of ascetics: when performed with material motives, it leads to non-dharma; but when performed without material motives, it leads to dharma.
What is *upadhā*?
“A defect in disposition (*bhāva*) is *upadhā*” (Pāṇini 6.2.4).
The meaning of *upadhi* is a defect such as hypocrisy (*dambha*) arising from the intention (*abhisandhi*) regarding one's state of being (*bhāva*).
What, then, is *anupadhi*?
“Absence of fault is *anupadhā*.
iv] The meaning is that *anupadhā* is the state of being free from deceit and the like within one’s intention (*abhisandhi*).
“That which possesses desirable form, taste, smell, and touch, and has been sprinkled and washed, is pure. (6.2.6)

That in which form and other qualities are not prohibited by tradition is pure, provided it has been sprinkled with water preceded by mantras or merely rinsed with pure water; that which is the opposite of this is impure.
Furthermore:
“‘Impure’ (aśuci) is the negation of purity.
(6.2.7) That which is an absolute negation of purity— such as foul speech and the like— is also impure.
“Another meaning. (6.2.8) [49,x]
Furthermore, that which is directly prohibited, such as intoxicants and the like, is also impure; therefore, one should consume what is pure.
[49,xi] Now, one might object:
“For one who is unrestrained, there is no spiritual progress from eating pure food, because of the absence of self-restraint.

(6.2.9) [49,xii] For one who is unrestrained— that is, devoid of a specific effort— and who consumes pure food by chance, there is no spiritual progress, due to the absence of a specific intention (*abhisandhi*).
This is not so,
because it exists as non-different from this [self], according to [the Sūtra]: "And it exists, because it is not a different thing from this" (6.2.10).
Restraint (yama) is not distinct from effort (prayatna), because in the absence of effort, all action would be non-existent; for one who partakes of pure food, effort exists.
If effort were the primary cause, then prosperity would occur even without yoga and the like. This is not so,
because "in its absence, there is no [result]" (6.2.11).
If there were no performance of yoga and so forth, spiritual prosperity would not arise from mere effort alone, because the instruction on ritual action would then be rendered useless.
Now, he states the dharma that is the cause of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa):
“From pleasure arises attachment.
(6.2.12) Attachment increases precisely from the pleasure produced by objects such as women.
“Because of being composed of that. (6.2.13)
By whichever causes of happiness this body has been cultivated, it remains as if composed of those very things; from that state of being composed of them, attachment arises. Furthermore:
“From satisfaction” (6.2.14).
When one becomes satisfied, then there arises in him, caused by that satisfaction, a passion for the nourishment of the body.
Furthermore: "From the unseen" (6.2.15).
[50,x] In the case of things never seen before and those that provide no benefit, the fact that attachment arises toward them has only the unseen (adṛṣṭa) as its cause.
Furthermore:
"And from the distinction of birth, there is a distinction of lineage.
Just as among animals there is attachment to the consumption of grass and so forth, so too does attachment arise from specific types of birth.
Attachment arises from pleasure and the like, while aversion arises from pain and the like. From that—

“Activity toward merit and demerit is preceded by desire and aversion” (6.2.17). Activity toward merit is preceded by desire; likewise, activity toward demerit may also be preceded by desire, as in the case of one overcome by the intoxication of wealth, or it may be preceded by aversion, as in the sacrifice for the sake of a village and the like. Toward demerit, activity is also preceded by desire, as in the case of another’s wife, or by aversion. In this way, there is the accumulation of merit and demerit.
Since this is so,
it follows that "from that [arise] conjunction and disjunction" (6.2.18).

When merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) have accumulated, then a conjunction with the body and the sense organs occurs, which is called birth; and when those two have been exhausted, at the time of death, there is a separation. Again, through these merits and demerits, there is a conjunction with the body and so forth, as well as a separation; in this way, this living being revolves without beginning like a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*).
This is stated in the reverse order, as follows: [51,i] Thus:—
“Liberation has been explained in relation to the actions of the self” (6.2.19).

Here, "self" refers to the mind (*manas*). Liberation has been explained as the absence of that [mind] in relation to mental actions, which results in the absence of conjunction and the non-manifestation [of suffering]. Thus, liberation has been explained.
<The Sixth Chapter> <The First Daily Lesson of the Seventh Chapter> [52,i]
Now he speaks of form and the other qualities:
"The qualities have been stated" (7.1.1).
The meaning is that they have been illustrated by the *Rūpādi-sūtra*.
[52,iii] "And the definition of the qualities (*guṇa*) has been stated. (7.1.2)
The meaning is that by the statement beginning with "dravyāśrayī" (1.1.15), its dissimilarity to substance and action is stated.
“And this has been stated as having such qualities, and that as having such qualities” (7.1.3).
For it has been said: “Earth possesses color, taste, smell, and touch” (2.1.1), and so forth.
In that regard:
"On earth, color, taste, smell, and touch are impermanent because their substance is impermanent. (7.1.4)
viii] Due to the destruction of an earthen substance such as a jar, there is also the destruction of the color and other qualities residing therein, because their substratum has been destroyed.
“And from contact with fire” (7.1.5).

Furthermore, due to contact with fire, there is the destruction of color and other qualities in the atoms of earth; however, in the case of those inherent in an effect, their destruction occurs solely through the destruction of their substrate.
[52,xi] Why is it that [destruction occurs] in atoms solely through contact with fire?
“Because of the manifestation of a different quality. (7.1.6)

[52,xii] Since another quality distinct from qualities such as blackness arises, therefore the previous qualities of the atoms have perished, because qualities do not originate in that which already possesses qualities.
[52,xiii]
“By this, impermanence is stated regarding eternal things.

(7.1.7) By this—namely, by the manifestation of another quality—the impermanence of color and other qualities in eternal atoms is stated; and this applies specifically to those atoms belonging to the earth.
For it is said:
“In water, fire, and air, [sound] is eternal because of the eternity of the substance. (7.1.8)

The color and other qualities of water, fire, air, and atoms are eternal because their substrata are eternal and because no opposing quality arises; therefore, there is no destruction through contact with fire.
[53,i] “In the case of non-eternal substances, they are non-eternal because the substance itself is non-eternal. (7.1.9)
[53,ii] In impermanent things such as water and so forth, form and the other [sensory qualities] are impermanent because they too perish when their substratum perishes.
“On earth, those produced by baking as well as those preceded by the qualities of the cause [arise].

(7.1.10) [53,iv] On impermanent earth, which is of the nature of an effect, qualities such as color arise preceded by the qualities of the cause; however, on eternal earth, which is of the nature of atoms, they are produced by baking—that is, born from the contact with fire through the process of baking.
“In water, fire, and air, the qualities produced by transformation (*pākaja*) do not exist as preceded by the qualities of their causes. (7.1.11)

In an effect that is a composite whole such as water, qualities such as color are originated in the form of inherent causes; however, qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) do not exist at all in the atoms of water and the like, because of the absence of any other opposing quality.
[53,vii] "Because qualities originate in a substance that is itself devoid of qualities, action and quality are themselves without qualities. (7.1.12)

[53.viii] Qualities are produced by the qualities of their causes only in the case of a substance that has arisen devoid of qualities, and not in the case of qualities or actions, because, like action, there is an absence of co-inherence in a single object with the qualities of all its constituent parts.

“By this, those produced by baking (*pākaja*) are explained. (7.1.13) [53,x] Since those qualities such as blackness (*śyāma*) cease upon contact with fire, those produced by baking arise; thus, they too are established as existing in that which is devoid of [prior] qualities.

If it is argued that, just as conjunction initiates another conjunction, so too do qualities produce qualities born of heating (*pākaja*), we say no, because [a substance] possesses only a single substance [as its substrate] (*ekadravyavattvāt*). (7.1.14)

[53,xii] Since those qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) reside in a single substance, how could they be initiated in that very same place? It would be contradictory. However, there is no fault in a conjunction being initiated in that which possesses conjunction, because it consists of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*).
[53,xiii]
Now we shall discuss dimension (*parimāṇa*):
"The perception and non-perception of the minute and the large have been explained in relation to the eternal. (NS 7.1.15) [53,xiv]

The term “in the eternal” (*nitye*) refers to the chapter [on the eternal]. “Whatever is perceived therein must necessarily possess magnitude; however, atoms, dyads, and the internal organ (*manas*) are not perceived despite being minute. Thus, in this chapter titled “The Eternal,” the causes of perception and non-perception—namely, magnitude (*mahattva*) and minuteness (*aṇutva*)—are stated, since magnitude is a necessary condition for perception. Although a triad (*tryaṇuka*) possesses magnitude, it is not perceived.
[54,i] “Magnitude [arises] from a plurality of causes, from the magnitude of the cause, and from a particular accumulation” (VS 7.1.16).

[54,ii] In a triad (*tryaṇuka*), the number of plurality residing in its cause, the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), produces magnitude (*mahattva*), because the causes themselves lack magnitude. In a two-fingered object, the magnitude of the finger that is the cause produces magnitude. Loose conjunction (*praśithila-saṃyoga*) is accumulation (*pracaya*). In a double-woolen blanket (*dvitūlaka*), the accumulation existing in the two tufts of wool, depending upon the loose conjunction of the parts of its own substratum, initiates magnitude.

"Minute is the opposite of that. (7.1.17) [54, iv] That dimension which is the opposite of the large [dimension] resulting from these three causes— the dimension of the dyad (dvyaṇuka)— is to be understood as minute (aṇu).
“[The notions of] ‘minute’ and ‘large’ [apply] to that [space], because of the presence of particularity and the absence of particularity. (7.1.18)

In that case, regarding a large object such as a *kuvala* fruit, there is the conventional usage of "minute" (*aṇu*) in comparison to an *āmalaka* fruit; however, the *āmalaka* itself is [regarded as minute] in comparison to a *bilva* fruit. Thus, due to the presence or absence of excellence (*prakarṣa*), the conventional usage of "minute" and "large" with respect to one and the same thing is merely figurative (*bhākta*).
Why is this so?
“Because they occur at the same time.

viii] Since, at one and the same time and with respect to that very same object, two persons perform the contradictory designations of "large" and "small" in relation to each other, we know from this that "this is figurative."
[54,ix] In that regard, concerning a relative minute object,
[it is said]: "And because of the example" (7.1.20).

[54,x] Just as in an effect produced from white threads there is only whiteness and not blackness, so too, by this analogy, in that which is begun by large [parts], there is only largeness and not minuteness. [54,xi]
“[The absence of minuteness and magnitude in minuteness and magnitude is explained by [the case of] actions and qualities.

(7.1.21) Just as qualities and actions are devoid of qualities because there is no inherence in a single substrate with the qualities of their constituent parts— as is the case with effects such as color— so too, because there is no inherence in a single substrate with the causes such as plurality, there is an absence of minuteness and magnitude in those two.
“Atomicity and magnitude, as well as actions and qualities, are themselves devoid of qualities. (7.1.22) [54,xiv]

Just as minuteness and magnitude are devoid of minuteness and magnitude themselves—due to the absence of co-inherence in a single object resulting from the multiplicity of causes and so forth—likewise, through action, they are devoid of minuteness and magnitude.
[55,i] "By this, length and shortness are explained. (7.1.23)

[55,ii] Perception and non-perception are like largeness and minuteness. Length arises from the largeness of the causes and so forth, while shortness arises from the opposite; because there is no distinction in that [substratum], its status as a figurative designation is likewise [the same]. The extension [of this principle] is that there is an absence of both length and shortness in those two [atoms]. [55,iii]
“Actions by actions, and qualities by qualities.

(7.1.24) [55, iv] Just as, due to the multiplicity of causes and the absence of inherence in a single object, these qualities of action are devoid of minuteness and magnitude, so too they are devoid of length and shortness.
“In that which is impermanent, it is impermanent. (7.1.25)
These four kinds of dimension are impermanent because they exist only in what is impermanent.
However—
“Spherical and eternal.
(7.1.26) [55, viii] The dimension of the atom is spherical, and that is eternal.
Regarding that:
“Ignorance is the mark of knowledge. (7.1.27)
The impossibility of a substance devoid of dimension is the mark for the existence of the atomic dimension of atoms. "Non-existence" is ignorance; "existence" is knowledge.
“Space is great because of its omnipresence.
(7.1.28) [55,xii] Because it does not come into contact with corporeal substances even when they meet, it is understood that space possesses supreme magnitude due to its conjunction with them.
“And so too is the self. (7.1.29) [55,xiv]

The self (ātman) should be regarded as supremely great, like space; since they are not composed of parts, space and time are also great. "Because of the absence of those [two], the mind is atomic" (7.1.30).
[55,xvi] Because of the absence of dissolution and because cognition is not simultaneous, the mind is atomic.
“Direction is explained by means of qualities.

(7.1.31) [56, ii] In whatever place one establishes a limit, there the conventional usage such as “this is to the east of that” and so forth proceeds with respect to corporeal objects; therefore, direction is explained by means of the qualities known as conjunctions with corporeal things, just like magnitude (*mahattva*).
Likewise: "By reason of the cause, it is time. (7.1.32)

Because time is inferred by means of such factors as the displacement of earlier and later [objects], and because that [inference] exists everywhere, for that very reason time is explained as all-pervading (*vibhu*).
[End of the First Daily Lesson of the Seventh Chapter]

[The Second Daily Lesson of the Seventh Chapter] [57,i] Now he begins the discussion of number and the other categories; number is the cause of the conventional usage of distinction. To show that it is distinct from color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest, he says:
“Unity is a distinct entity, different from color, taste, smell, and touch; likewise is separateness. (7.2.1) [57,ii]

The cognition "this is one," and so forth, does not have color (*rūpa*) and other such qualities as its cause, because it is distinct in character from the cognitions of those [qualities]. For the cognition of color and so on would take the form "possessing color" (*rūpavān*), and so forth. Therefore, it must have a different object as its cause. Unity (*ekatva*) and individual separateness (*eka-pṛthaktva*) in effects are preceded by the qualities of their causes. Duality (*dvitva*) and so forth are produced from unities accompanied by a cognition of multiple objects. Likewise, duality of separateness (*dvi-pṛthaktva*) and so forth are produced from instances of separateness; however, there is no lower generality (*apara-sāmānya*) for unity of separateness and the like.
“Their [unity and separateness] being eternal or non-eternal is explained by [the same criteria as] light, namely by its color and touch.

(7.2.2) Just as light-atoms are eternal because their substance is eternal, and thus their color and touch are likewise eternal, so too are unity and separateness eternal when they reside in an eternal substance; and just as in non-eternal light, unity and separateness are non-eternal because their substance is non-eternal, so too are unity and separateness non-eternal when they reside in an effect-substance.
“And accomplishment. (7.2.3) [57, vi]

And just as in the case of fire, the production of color and touch occurs preceded by the qualities of the cause, so too is it for oneness and separateness. The same applies to heaviness, substantiality, and viscidity.
[57, vii] “The absence of oneness and separateness in oneness and separateness is explained by the [discussion of] minuteness and magnitude. (7.2.4)
The meaning is that because of the absence of inherence in a single object with respect to the parts and the quality, oneness and separateness do not exist.
“Actions by means of actions, and qualities by means of qualities.
(7.2.5) [57,x] Likewise, because there is no inherence in a single object between parts and qualities, actions and qualities do not possess unity or separateness.

[57,xi] But surely all categories of entities must possess oneness, since they are not distinguished by their existence; for it is said: “Because actions and qualities lack number, there is no oneness of all things” (7.2.6).
[57,xii] Because actions and qualities are devoid of numerical enumeration, there is no such thing as the oneness of all things.
[57,xiii]
If it is argued that oneness regarding qualities and so forth is figurative, [the reply is:
“Because oneness does not exist, there can be no figurative usage.

Since a primary oneness does not exist, the figurative oneness that is postulated for qualities and so forth is insufficient for the establishment of your [proposed] oneness; for precisely because of this, there would follow the consequence of a distinction between them, namely: "oneness is primary in substances, while it is figurative in qualities. [57,xv] Now, one might object: "Oneness must apply to cause and effect, because number is indistinguishable in a substance; and due to the very absence of oneness, there would likewise be an absence of separateness. This is not so.
“Because of the absence of identity and difference between cause and effect, unity and plurality do not exist.
(7.2.8) [57,xvi] Due to the duality of cause and effect, there is no identity; nor is there plurality, because the effect lacks a substratum distinct from the cause.
[57,xvii] “This has been explained regarding the impermanent and the permanent. (7.2.9) [57,xviii]

This preceding sūtra, although having impermanent objects as its domain, should be understood as explained as applicable as far as possible even to permanent entities such as space (*ākāśa*). For instance: "Conjunction is produced by the action of one of two things, by the action of both, or by conjunction. (7.2.10) Furthermore, there is neither identity nor separateness between sound and space, which stand in the relation of effect and cause. [57,xix]

[57,xx] There is conjunction of a non-eternal action with a stationary object, as in the case of a hawk’s act of swooping down upon a post; there is that which arises from both, as in the case of two wrestlers’ act of approaching one another. Conjunction produced by conjunction occurs when there is a conjunction between a cause and a non-cause, resulting in a conjunction between the effect and a non-effect, such as the conjunction of two fingers with space resulting from the two conjunctions of the individual fingers with space.

“By this, the classification [of disjunction] is explained” (7.2.11). Disjunction produced by the action of one [of two things] occurs from the moving away of a hawk. Disjunction produced by the action of both occurs from the moving away of two rams. But disjunction produced by disjunction [itself] occurs, for example, when the disjunction between two fingers has just ceased, there arises the disjunction of the finger from space; or, from the disjunction of the hand and space—the cause and non-cause—there arises the disjunction of the body and space.

[57,xxiii] “The absence of conjunction and disjunction in conjunction and disjunction has been explained by [the absence of] minuteness and magnitude. (7.2.12) The meaning is that because there is no separate existence (*yutasiddhi*), those two do not exist.
“By actions, actions; by qualities, qualities. (7.2.13)
The meaning is that because there is no separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*), they do not possess conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or disjunction (*vibhāga*).
[59,iii] “Because of the absence of separate establishment, conjunction and disjunction do not exist between cause and effect. (7.2.14)

[59, iv] Between cause and effect, there is no mutual conjunction or disjunction, as in the case of a jar and its shards, because of the absence of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*). Separate existence consists in either both or one of two things possessing distinct motion; this applies to eternal things. For non-eternal things, it consists in inherence in different substrates, as in the case of a jar and a cloth, or the sense-organ of touch and the earthly body. However, there is no inherence in different substrates between a jar and its shards, because the jar inheres in those very shards themselves.
If it is argued that there is a relationship between the word and its meaning, no;
because [the suffix] is a quality (*guṇatvāt*). (Pāṇini 5.2.15) [59, vi]
Because sound is a quality of space, it is not connected with its referent;
for it is stated: "And [the suffix] is used in the sense of a quality" (Pāṇini 5.2.16).

[59, viii] Furthermore, in expressions such as "the taste is first," the term is employed for both a quality (*guṇa*) and an action (*kriyā*); yet there is no connection between qualities and actions on the one hand and qualities on the other.
“Because it is devoid of action. (7.2.17) [59,x] If there were a conjunction with an object, the word might reach that object; however, because a quality is devoid of action, there is no movement.
“Because of the application [of the terms] ‘when it is not, it does not exist’” (7.2.18).

When there is a connection with an object, the word "exists" is used; when it is "not existing," that is, in the case of absence, the word "does not exist" would not be applied. For there is no connection with what is non-existent.
Therefore, because of the absence of such a connection—
“Word and meaning are unconnected.
(7.2.19) But surely—
“From the staff which is conjoined, and from the horn which is inherent” (7.2.20).

It is observed that the cognition of the possessor of the staff and the possessor of the horn arises from the staff and the horn, which are respectively conjoined and inherent. And since there is a cognition of an object from a word, it follows that this [word] also possesses a relationship [to its object].
[60,iii] This is not so:
"Because it is observed, the condition is not a cause" (7.2.21).

[60, iv] There is no fault [in our position] because the relationship between a staff-bearer and a horned animal is observed; however, in this case, since the relationship between word and meaning is not observed according to the reasoning already stated, the cognition of the meaning is not based on a [real] relationship.
“Likewise, there is an absence of conditions.
(7.2.22) [60, vi] If a word were connected with its object, then even one who has not grasped the convention would understand the object from it; therefore, they are unconnected.
“If it is argued that [the inference is established] because of a connection with what is connected, there is doubt. (7.2.23)

[Objection: But surely the word is connected with space, and the object is connected with space; thus, through this connection of connections, there is a connection with the object. [Response: This is not so. Since all objects are connected with space, there would be non-comprehension due to doubt as to which specific object the word has been employed for. Therefore, there is no connection. Consequently—
“The cognition of an object from a word is conventional” (7.2.24).
Therefore, the cognition of an object from a word is caused by convention (*saṃketa*), not by an inherent relation (*sambandha*).
“By means of direction and time that are proximate and remote, respectively, there is ‘far’ and ‘near. (7.2.25)

Two objects situated in the same direction are the cause of priority and posteriority produced by spatial direction (*dik*). Two objects existing at the same time, connected to the present time, are the cause of priority and posteriority produced by time (*kāla*). And those two objects are the cause [of these qualities] insofar as they depend upon the cognitions of being near (*sannikṛṣṭa*) or far (*viprakṛṣṭa*).
[61,i] “Because of the priority of the cause and because of the posteriority of the cause. (7.2.26)

[61, ii] Conjunction with spatial regions that are distant or proximate is the non-inherent cause [of the notions of priority and posteriority]. Likewise are conjunctions with temporal regions that are distant or proximate. Due to conjunction with spatial and temporal regions, in relation to two objects—one near and one far—the notion of proximity arises in the near object and the notion of distance in the far object; based on these notions of proximity and distance, there is "posteriority" (aparatva) in the near object and "priority" (paratva) in the far object.
“The absence of remoteness and proximity in [the qualities of] remoteness and proximity is explained by [the absence of] minuteness and magnitude.

(7.2.27) [61, iv] Conjunctions with points of space and time that are remote or proximate are the causes of remoteness and proximity. Since these two [qualities] lack co-inherence (*yutasiddhi*), there is an absence of conjunction; therefore, there is an absence of remoteness and proximity.
“Actions by means of actions, and qualities by means of qualities. (7.2.28)

Just as the qualities of action (*karmaguṇa*) are devoid of minuteness and magnitude, so too, due to the absence of separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*) through action, they lack conjunction with points of space and time, and are thus devoid of priority and posteriority.
[61,vii] “That from which the relation ‘here’ exists between cause and effect is inherence (*samavāya*). (7.2.29)

[61.viii] Qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are inherent (*samavāyin*) in substance (*dravya*). Therefore, he explains inherence (*samavāya*): that from which the cognition "here" arises with respect to cause and effect—such as "the cloth is here in the threads" or "action is here in the jar"—that is inherence. Since the mention of "cause and effect" is illustrative, it is thereby stated that "there is inherence of the universal (*jāti*) in the individual (*vyakti*), and of particulars (*viśeṣa*) in eternal substances.
“The negation of substance-ness, quality-ness, and action-ness is explained by means of existence (bhāva).

(7.2.30) Just as existence is not a substance because it inheres in a single substance, and is neither an action nor a quality because it exists in qualities and actions, so too is inherence (samavāya).
"And reality," (7.2.31).

Just as there is one entity because there is no distinction in its true marks, so too, because there is no distinction in its marks here, inherence (samavāya) is one; it is devoid of occurrence, eternal, and partless.
[Thus ends the seventh chapter.
[The eighth chapter begins.]
i] Intellect (*buddhi*) is now being examined: "Knowledge with respect to substances has been explained" (8.1).
[62,ii] Among the six types of objects for the sake of others, cognition regarding substances alone has been explained as arising from contact; however, this does not apply to qualities and so forth.
Of that [person]: "The mind and the self. (8.2) [62,iv]
The mind and the self have been explained as the causes of cognition. Now, he describes cognition regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth:
“In the exposition of knowledge, the production of knowledge has been stated.

(8.3) Since the production of knowledge through the contact of the sense-faculties has been stated, and since there is no contact of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth with the sense-faculty, let knowledge now be discussed.
vii] Since their non-contact [with the sense organs] results in cognition—
“Because knowledge arises with respect to qualities and actions that are not in contact [with the senses], substance is the cause and the cause of the cause. (8.4)

[62, viii] Since substance is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of qualities and actions, when these [qualities and actions] are not in direct contact with the sense organ, it is that very substance which is the cause for the production of cognition regarding them, and not the qualities or actions themselves. Therefore, in the case of qualities and actions, cognition arises through "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*); the word "and" (*ca*) indicates the reason.
“Because there is an absence of further universals and particulars within universals and particulars, cognition of them is of that very same kind.

(8.5) [62,x] Regarding universals such as *sattā* and the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*), for those who perceive them, cognition arises from the mere contact with the substance itself, not from further universals or particulars, because they are absent in them.
But elsewhere it is said:
"In the case of substances, qualities, and actions, there is dependence on both the universal and the particular. (8.6)

[63, ii] With respect to substances, qualities, and actions, from the contact of the substance with the sense organ, and from the universal (*sāmānya*) such as *sattā* (existence), and from the particular universals (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) such as *dravyatva* (substanceness), there arises the cognition "existent" and "substance," and so forth. In this sūtra, the universal is *sattā*, while the particulars are *dravyatva* and the like; in the previous sūtra, it was otherwise.
In that regard as well:
“With respect to a substance, it depends on substance, quality, and action. (8.7) [63, iv]

The cognition that arises from the contact of the eye with a substance—such as "it has horns" when dependent on a universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), "it is white" when dependent on a quality (*guṇa*), or "it moves" when dependent on an action (*karman*)—occurs in this way. Furthermore, because substances and the like function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), they are apprehended first; therefore, the cognition of the qualifier is the cause and the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is the effect.
[63,v] "In the case of qualities and actions, because there is an absence of further qualities and actions, there is no dependence upon [further] qualities or actions. (8.8)

vi] Because there is an absence of quality and action within a quality, and because there is an absence of quality and action within an action, there is no cognition of qualities and actions caused by qualities and actions.
There is no fixed rule regarding the prior arising of cognition with respect to substance and so forth; for example:
“From the whiteness inherent [in a substance], through the cognition of whiteness, there arises a cognition of the white [substance]; these two stand in the relation of cause and effect.

From the inherence of the quality of whiteness and from the cognition of the generality of whiteness, the cognition of the quality of whiteness arises; the connection with the generality and the quality must also be observed. Therefore, the cognition of the qualifier is the cause, and the cognition of the qualified is the effect.
However, in the absence of the relationship between qualifier and qualified—
“Because substances do not act as causes for one another, and because causes do not arise simultaneously.

(8.10) [63,x] Due to the atomicity of the mind, there is an absence of simultaneity; thus, even though there is a sequence between the cognitions of a jar and a cloth, they do not stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, because it is impossible for them to function as qualifier and qualified.
“Likewise, with respect to substances, qualities, and actions, because there is no distinction in their causes. (8.11)

In the case of "The white cow goes," even though cognitions of substance, quality, and action arise sequentially, there is no relation of cause and effect between them because there is no relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatā*); this is due to the fact that the previously stated reason remains unchanged. Therefore, the cognition of a substance is not the cause of the cognitions of quality and action, nor are the cognitions of quality and action the cause of the other.
However, in the absence of the principle of the qualifier—
“This one here has been done by you; feed him”—this depends upon cognition.

(8.12) [64, ii] The notion “this one” (*ayam*) refers to what is proximate, while “that one” (*eṣaḥ*) refers to what is somewhat remote. In “done by you” (*kṛtaṃ tvayā*), there are the notions of object and agent; in “feed him” (*bhojayainam*), there are the notions of agent and object. The notion regarding the remote depends upon the proximate; in “done,” the notion of the agent depends upon the object; in “feed,” the notion of the object depends upon the agent.
If it is asked, "Why are they dependent?
[the answer is]: "Because they exist when [the conditions] are seen, and they do not exist when they are not seen. (8.13)

[64,iv] Since cognitions of "remote" and so forth arise only with respect to things that are seen and proximate, and not with respect to things that are unseen, they are therefore dependent; yet, even while being dependent, they do not stand in the relation of cause and effect, because it is impossible for them to function as qualifier and qualified.
Although cognitions depend upon both objects and the sense organs, the object is first discussed:
"The term 'object' (artha) refers to substances, qualities, and actions" (8.14).

Even in the absence of a common property such as "object-ness" (*arthatva*), the word "object" (*artha*) is conventionally defined (*paribhāṣyate*) with reference to those three categories—substance and the rest—because it is well-established therein. Where is this so? Just as among generalities and particularities there is the cognition "generality, generality" even in the absence of another overarching generality—as in the case of generalities such as "existence" (*sattā*)—and just as among particularities there is the cognition of those who perceive them, "particularity, particularity," despite the absence of another particularity; in the same way, the word "object" is used conventionally for substance and the other categories even in the absence of the property of object-ness.
[64, vii] The sense organs are mentioned; and they are not composed of the five elements, because—
“Regarding substances, that which consists of five elements has been refuted” (8.15).
Since, among substances that are to be produced, the five primary elements do not exist as producers; rather, those four which produce [a substance] each produce their own respective genus.
In the same way, the sense organs are also effects of specific elements; thus it is said:
“Earth predominates in the cognition of smell because of its abundance and its possession of fragrance. (8.16)

[64,x] Olfactory cognition is the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*). When that is to be produced, earth is the cause because of its predominance; this predominance, however, is relative to the body. Furthermore, earth predominates in the sense of smell because there is no perception of odor by means of the feet and so forth. Moreover, because it possesses odor, and since the olfactory faculty manifests odor through the odor inherent within itself, earth alone—possessing odor—is its cause; the other elements, while present in conjunction, exist only in minute quantities. [65,i]
“Likewise, water, fire, and air [are distinguished] by the specificities of taste, form, and touch within the cognitions of taste, form, and touch. (8.17) [65,ii]

Because the tongue, the eye, and the sense of touch manifest taste, color, and touch respectively—by means of their own inherent (samavāyin) taste produced by post-origination cooking (*apākaja*), by color that is white and brilliant, and by touch that is neither hot nor cold produced by post-origination cooking—it should be understood that, due to the predominance of water, fire, and air respectively, caused by their non-overpowering by other elements, these three elements serve as the inherent causes (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) for the three sense organs. However, space itself is the auditory organ (*śrotra*) when delimited by the ear-cavity; it is not the material cause (*prakṛti*), because it does not initiate [the production of] effects. Thus, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has been explained.
<The Eighth Chapter> <The Ninth Chapter> [66,i]
Now, wishing to explain inference (*anumāna*), he shows its object:
"It is non-existent because of the absence of designation by action or quality" (9.1).

Prior to its production, that [non-existent thing] cannot be grasped by perception; nor can it be grasped by inference, because inference exists only when there is a mark (*liṅga*), and there is an absence of such a mark due to the non-apprehension of its action and qualities. Furthermore, there is no other mark indicated by the word "designation" (*vyapadeśa*). Therefore, prior to production, it is non-existent.
As for what follows—
“Both existent and non-existent.

(9.2) [66,iv] An effect that has truly come into being, once destroyed at a later time, is simply non-existent; it is not a case of the concealment of the existent, precisely because there is an absence of activity, qualities, and designation.
But in the middle [of the treatise]:
"Because of the absence of activity, qualities, and designation for that which is non-existent, it is a different entity" (9.3).

vi] Prior to its destruction and subsequent to its arising, an entity that was previously non-existent is called "existent" because it is a distinct thing, owing to the presence of activity, qualities, and designations. [66, vii]
“‘Non-existent’ (asat):

(9.4) Even an existent thing (*sat*) is designated as ‘non-existent’ by way of negating its being another entity— for instance, when one says, “A cow is not a horse”— or by way of its causal function, as in, “This cow does not carry [the load],” where it is figuratively termed ‘non-existent.’
“And whatever else exists, that too is non-existent. (9.5)

Furthermore, that which is other than an existent entity—namely, that which consists of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), such as a rabbit's horn, which is not the object of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)—is also simply non-existent (*asat*). If it is asked: "Since there is no distinction among non-existent things, how can the activity of causal factors (*kāraka*) occur in the case of prior non-existence and not elsewhere?", we reply: No, because a distinction is perceived.
Regarding this: [67,i] Therein—
“[The cognition] ‘it is non-existent’ arises from the absence of perception of the existing thing, from the memory of that existing thing, and from the perception of its opposite.

(9.6) Regarding non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsāsati*), the cognition “it is non-existent” arises by postulating destruction because there is currently no perception of the previously existing object as it was before, because of the recollection of that existing object, and because of the apprehension of its opposite, such as the potsherds; for otherwise, how could it not be seen, since there would be no difference in its state?
Regarding prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), however: “Because there is the perception of existence when such [prior non-existence] is absent. (9.7)

[67, iv] In the state of the lump of clay, there was no perceptual cognition regarding the jar due to its prior non-existence; now, however, a contradictory cognition regarding the jar has arisen, and the state of non-existence is remembered. Therefore, one concludes: "Now this entity has come into being, whereas previously it was indeed non-existent. Thus, regarding prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), there is the determinative cognition that "it was non-existent. [67, v]
“By this, the non-pot, the non-cow, and the non-property are explained.

For when, in the case of one who has produced the cognition "a jar" regarding a pot, a correct cognition arises from another cause—"This is not a jar; this is a pot"—that too is to be understood as such because of the absence of the cognition of "jar," because of the memory of that [prior cognition], and because of the perception of the contradictory object, the pot and so forth. Likewise, in the case of a horse, there is the cognition "not a cow. Similarly, if through general observation bathing at night and so forth are suspected of being *dharma*, the cognition "this is non-*dharma*" arises. These are three examples distinguished by their objects: sentient, insentient, and beyond the senses.
“‘Non-existent’ (*abhūta*) and ‘does not exist’ (*nāsti*) are not different in meaning.

(9.9) [67, viii] That which is of the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), such as a rabbit’s horn—which exists prior to, after, or independent of conditions—is expressed by the synonymous terms (*paryāya-śabda*) ‘non-existent’ and ‘does not exist’ as being non-distinct from them; its difference in meaning from these synonymous terms is not asserted. Therefore, its definition is its demonstration by means of those very synonymous terms, and not a negation of it in terms of place, time, and so forth.
But elsewhere it is said:
“In the statement ‘there is no jar in the house,’ there is a negation of the connection with the house of an existing jar. (9.10)
[68,ii] "There is no jar in this place or at this time" is a negation of the jar and so forth with respect to place and the like; it is not a negation made with respect to its own essential nature.

“There is no other moon”: this is a negation of the moon by way of its universal (*sāmānya*). (9.11) [68, iv] By means of the negation of number—namely, “there is no second moon”—the moon is excluded from what is called its moon-ness (*candratva*) as a universal; thus, it is effectively stated that the universal of moon-ness does not exist. They explain that when the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of place, time, state, and capacity are absent, there is a negation of the universal of moon-ness, which is an absolute non-entity (*atyantāsattva*) in terms of its particularity.
Because curd does not arise from the pot, yet arises from milk, and because it is not perceived [as existing] through direct perception, the effect exists and does not exist within the cause.
“Because of the difference in nature between existence and non-existence, there is neither existence nor non-existence in the effect.
(9.12) Since existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory at the same time, the effect is neither existent nor non-existent in the cause; therefore, it is simply non-existent.
[68, viii] Because its objects are both perceptible and imperceptible, the perception of the yogin is explained between perception and inference:
“The perception of the self arises from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind within the self. (9.13)

ix] When the sense organs are withdrawn from their objects and the mind is concentrated upon the self alone, then, due to the conjunction of the self and the internal organ— which is distinguished by its dependence on the dharma born of yoga— there arises for the venerable ones a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of their own self.
“Likewise with other substances” (9.14).

Cognition arises in respect to pervasive substances whose conjunction with the self is prohibited— since they are not conjoined with the self— and also in respect to atoms and so forth, whose conjunction with the self is not prohibited, since they are conjoined with both.
Furthermore: “And from the contact of the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the objects. (9.15)
[69,ii] In the case of objects that are subtle, concealed, or remote, their perception arises even from the contact of the fourfold [causes]; likewise in the perceptions of people such as ourselves.
“Because of inherence in that [substance], [cognition arises] with respect to actions and qualities.

(9.16) Just as cognition arises in other substances due to conjunction with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), so too does cognition arise with respect to the actions and qualities inherent in those same substances. And just as cognition arises regarding subtle objects and so forth—which are perceptible to us—due to the fourfold contact (*catuṣṭaya-sannikarṣa*), so too does cognition arise with respect to the qualities and actions inherent in them, by means of "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-samavāya*).
“[Cognition arises] with respect to the qualities of the self through inherence in the self. (9.17)

Just as knowledge arises within one's own self through the conjunction of the self and the mind, in exactly the same way, knowledge arises regarding pleasure and other qualities inherent in that very self.
Having explained yogic perception, he now explains inference: [69,vii]
“‘This is the effect of that, this is the cause of that, this is related to that, this is inherent in the same object as that, and this is contradictory to that’—this is inferential knowledge.

Having shown the mere relationship in the form "this belongs to that," he specifies it by means of the terms "effect" and "cause," and so forth. By the mention of "effect and cause," there is an inclusion of genus (*jāti*) and other categories as well, since they are indicated by their inherent relationship (*samavāyin*); by the word "related" (*sambandhin*), there is the inclusion of things joined by conjunction (*saṃyogin*), such as smoke and the like. The rest has been explained in the *Sūtra* on "the related" (*saṃyogyādi*). Regarding this, the author of the *Vṛtti* states: "When one perceives an unmistakable part of an object belonging to such a well-known relationship, the subsequent cognition of the remainder which arises from the perception of the mark (*liṅga*) is inferential (*laiṅgika*). [69, ix]
“By this, verbal cognition (*śabda*) is explained.

(9.19) Just as inference—which depends on the recollection of the relationship between cause and effect and so forth—has objects belonging to the three times and transcends the senses, so too does verbal cognition depend on the recollection of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), has objects belonging to the three times, and transcends the senses. Therefore, because it shares the same status (*ekayogakṣema*) as inference, it is said to be nothing other than inference.
[69,xi] If you ask what word denotes "the object" (*artha*), it is said:
"Cause (*hetu*), indicator (*apadeśa*), mark (*liṅga*), sign (*nimitta*), means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and reason (*kāraṇa*) are synonymous. (9.20)
By means of words such as "reason" (*hetu*) and so forth, he speaks of the cause with primary intent. The meaning of "reason," "indication" (*apadeśa*), and "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is the same.
If it is asked: why is the word "thus" (*evam*) a sign (*liṅga*) for the comprehension of an existing object? [70,i]
“Because it depends upon the cognition that ‘this belongs to that’.

Just as when there is an established convention (*vṛtta-saṅketa*) such that "this hand gesture is to be understood as the cause for the comprehension of this meaning," one perceives the meaning from that word-cause upon seeing that hand gesture; likewise, when there is a well-known convention (*prasiddha-saṅketa*) such that "this word is the cause for the comprehension of this meaning," one perceives the meaning from that word-cause. Just as worldly people perceive meaning even from gestures and the like, so too the Commentator [holds] that the word is the cause of the meaning because it manifests it by virtue of convention. In this way, [the other means of knowledge] such as comparison (*upamāna*) are included [within these two]. Thus, there are only two means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And as for the state of being a means of knowledge: it is a *pramāṇa* because "by this [means] something is correctly measured" (*pramīyate*), or else it is a *pramāṇa* because it is the "instrument of correct cognition" (*pramā*).
[70,iii] Memory is said to be a constituent factor of inference: “Memory arises from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, and from latent impressions. (9.22)

[70,iv] For one who desires fire, once the perception of smoke has arisen, there arises from the contact of the self with the internal organ—dependent upon that [perception]—and from a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*) called *bhāvanā*, the memory: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire.
“Likewise, dream and the state following a dream” (9.23).

Dream is the cognition of one whose sense organs have ceased to function and whose mind has dissolved, occurring through the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone. Within a dream, the cognition of a dream is the "state following a dream" (*svapnāntika*). Both of these arise from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, which depends on prior cognitions and is assisted by mental impressions (*bhāvanā*).
“And from the Dharma. (9.24) [70,
viii]

Even dream-cognition, though having as its object a thing not previously experienced, is an indicator of what is auspicious or inauspicious due to *dharma*; and by the word "and" (*ca*), it is also due to *adharma*.
But for one who is awake—
“Nescience arises from a defect of the sense organs and from mental impressions” (9.25).

For one whose sense organs are impaired by a defect such as wind (*vāta*), there arises—due to a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, depending on demerit (*adharma*) and upon a mental impression produced by a previous experience of that same object—the cognition of something as being what it is not, such as [the cognition] of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) is, for example, like a Southerner’s perception of a camel.
[71,i] “That is faulty cognition.
That which is characterized by doubt, error, non-apprehension, and dreaming is defective and thus invalid. [71,iii] “The non-defective is valid knowledge. (9.27)
iv] That which is non-defective, known as perception and inference, is called *vidyā* (knowledge).
“The vision of the ṛṣis and the vision of the perfected ones arise from the dharmas.

In this regard, that intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) which arises for the divine seers (*devarṣis*) concerning past, future, and present objects—such as *dharma* and so forth—which are beyond the senses and not conveyed by verbal texts, and which occurs only occasionally for ordinary people (e.g., "My brother will come tomorrow," or "My heart tells me so"), having as its fruit a lack of certainty and being guided solely by reasoning, is called *ārṣa*. Furthermore, that knowledge concerning subtle, hidden, or remote objects belonging to those perfected through ointments, elixirs, and the like; or the thorough discernment of the ripening of the merit and demerit of living beings based on celestial, atmospheric, and other omens—that is *siddhadarśana*. They describe this as not differing from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), whereas it does differ from *ārṣa*. Both this *ārṣa* and *siddhadarśana* arise from a specific *dharma* and from the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga*).
Thus ends the ninth chapter.
The tenth chapter.

While the discussion regarding the intellect (*buddhi*) has not yet reached its conclusion, he speaks of pleasure and pain as the objects of pleasure and pain; for instance, he says, "The elements consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion," and so forth. That is incorrect.
[72,ii] "The inherence in the self (*ātmasamavāya*) is the reason for pleasure and pain being distinct from the five [elements], and also from those qualities that reside in them. (10.1)

[72, iii] That inherence which belongs to pleasure, pain, and so forth, within the self (*ātman*) itself is the reason for their being distinct entities from the five elements—earth and the rest—which serve as their substrata, as well as from the qualities of smell, taste, color, and touch; for the qualities of one thing do not inhere in another. Furthermore, the inherence of these two [pleasure and pain] in the self is established by their forming a single syntactical unit with the notion of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*).
Even if they were inherent in the self—
[72,v] “Because of the distinction between the causes of the desired and the undesired, and because of their mutual opposition, pleasure and pain are different entities. (10.2)

[72, vi] Pleasure is produced by causes such as women; pain is produced by causes such as poison. Furthermore, pleasure and pain are mutually contradictory because they arise through the destruction of one another. Therefore, there is a distinction between these two; they are not identical, despite their inherence in a single substratum.
If it is argued that doubt and certainty are merely mutual absences and do not exist as real entities, we say no;
for [it is stated]: "The fact that doubt and certainty are distinct objects is the reason for their being different cognitions" (10.3).

The arising (*bhāva*) or production of doubt and certainty occurs from a distinct cause (*arthāntara*) that is mutually different. To explain: for one who desires to know a particularity but has not yet grasped it, doubt arises from the perception of a general feature. Following that doubt, through the apprehension of the particularity by means of another instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there arises the certainty: "This is indeed a post. If these two were not real entities, they would not be produced from such distinct causes. Therefore, some maintain that doubt and certainty are distinct types of cognition from one another, yet certainty does not differ from perception and inference.
“The accomplishment of these two has been explained by means of the two types of knowledge: perception and that which is based on a logical mark. (10.4)

Just as, having seen a perceptible mark (*liṅga*) of the self that is remembered, knowledge arises regarding that which is imperceptible, so too, from the perception of a mere generality (*sāmānyamātra*), for one who possesses memory and desires to know the particular (*viśeṣa*), there arises a doubt—"Is it a post or a person?"—so long as the particular has not been grasped. And just as perceptual knowledge arises through the force of a connection with a real object (*bhūtārtha*) such that "this object is of such a nature," so too, when the doubt has ceased through the force of a connection with the particular, a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) arises such that "this is of such a nature.
Now he defines the cognitions of effect and cause:
“‘It is an existent thing’—this explains perception.

When an effect has arisen from its own causes, the cognition that "this effect is produced" (*bhūta*) or "this effect is accomplished" (*niṣpanna*) is the cognition of the effect; this is explained according to the principle that "from the cognition of the qualifier arises the cognition of the qualified," and it is primary (*mukhya*). In other cases, however, it is figurative (*aupacārika*), because of the absence of an actual effect. For instance, when an effect is yet to be produced (*niṣpatsyamāne kārye*)—
“It will come to be, because it has been seen in other instances of an effect” (10.6).

Just as an effect such as a cloth is seen to arise immediately after a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of a certain kind, so too, by observing a causal complex of that same kind, even when the effect has not yet arisen, one applies the term "effect" metaphorically and the cognition of an "effect" arises, thinking, “the effect will come to be.”
Even when it is being produced—
"it becomes thus" from those that are dependent and from those that are independent. (10.7)

[73, vi] When one does not perceive the previously extended threads as depending on their prior conjunctions, but subsequently perceives them as independent upon the occurrence of each successive conjunction with a later thread— then, for one who observes an intermediate product such as a strip of cloth while a substantial effect is being produced, the cognition arises that "the effect exists" and "the effect is produced," through the process of enumerating the conjunctions of the already produced and the yet-to-be-produced.

Just as it was explained regarding origination, so too regarding destruction: for substances such as jars that arise immediately after an effort, the cognition "it was" (*abhūt*) [is established] because of the absence of perception of what has come into being (*bhūtapratyakṣābhāvāt*), as stated in verse 9.6. Now, this is discussed with respect to transformational things such as the body. In that regard, when something has perished:
"from what has been, [the notion] 'it was' arises" (10.8).

"From what has not come into being" means from what has perished. Having perceived the separated parts—the hands, feet, neck, and so forth—from the conjunction which is the non-inherent cause having perished, when the effect has perished, the cognition arises: "The effect called the body no longer exists.
It perishes again—
“And because, even if it exists, it does not inhere in the effect.

When there is contact—or by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), when there is no contact—even though the operation of causes of destruction such as a killer has occurred, because the contact of certain neck-parts has not ceased while the contact of the hands and so forth has ceased due to disjunction, the cognition "the effect is destroyed" arises from observing the contact that is both destroyed and not destroyed, on account of the non-inherence of the effect, such as the body, and because it has been set in motion by the cause of its destruction. Others, however, explain it as "the effect has come to be non-existent" (*abhūt*); that is incorrect, because according to that very intention, the effect is indeed destroyed. And this is the cognition:
[74,iii] And this is the cognition—
“Because it is observed among other causes that are inherent in a single object, [the term] ‘one part’ refers to one [of them].

(10.10) [74,iv] When parts such as the hand and so forth are perceived as inherent in some single object, such as a body, then the cognition of “one part” arises with respect to those [parts]; subsequently, having distinguished and perceived those [parts] as distinct, there arises the cognition regarding that whole (*ekadeśin*) that “the effect has come into being.”
"What are those parts? he says: "The head, back, belly, and hands—from their specific varieties" (10.11).

The meaning is that those parts, such as the head and so forth, from which cognition arises by means of their own specific and general characteristics, such as "head-ness" and so on, are the parts like the head. [74,vii]
But the cognition of "cause" is as follows: "It is called a cause because the effect is inherent in the substance" (10.12).
[74, viii]

For one who perceives an effect— whether it be a substance, a quality, or an action— as inhering in a substance, there arises the primary cognition that "the substance is the cause," because the effect has already come into being.
But when the effect has not yet arisen—
“Because of conjunction.
(10.13) Even when the effect is yet to be produced, because of the mutual conjunction of the threads and so forth, the cognition of them as causes with respect to this cloth arises.
[75,iii] “From the conjunction of causes, [the cognition arises] with respect to the action.

Because it is the independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions, and because it inheres in the substance that is its cause, action, as soon as it arises, produces the cognition of its cause. Now, regarding qualities—
“Likewise, with respect to color (*rūpa*), it is due to inherence in the cause of the cause.

(10.15) [75, vi] Because they inhere in those causes of the cause—the threads which are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the cloth and so forth, which are the inherent causes of the color that is the effect—they are called the causes of color and so forth. By the word “and” (*ca*), it is indicated that even when the color of the effect has not yet arisen, there is still the cognition of it as a cause.
“[The cognition of] conjunction arises from the inherence of its causes.

Because an effect such as a cloth is inherent (*samaveta*) in its inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*), such as the threads, there arises the notion of a cause with respect to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) regarding the substance.
However, in the case of the initiation of qualities and actions—
“Likewise, due to inherence in both the cause and the non-cause” (10.17).

In the case of qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*), the conjunction with fire is the cause because it inheres in the jar, which is the cause, and in the fire, which is not the cause. Similarly, the conjunction of substances is the cause of action because it inheres in the object struck, which is the cause of the action, and in the striker, which is not the cause—just as in the case of sound.
But regarding the commencement of that which is produced by ripening (*pākaja*), [it is said]: "The specific quality of fire [arises] through inherence in what is conjoined" (VS 10.18).

[75,xii] In the production of color and other qualities born of baking (*pākaja*) in atoms, the conjunction depends upon the specific quality (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*) of heat-contact inherent in the fire conjoined with those atoms. With the exception of substance (*dravya*), conjunction is a dependent cause in other cases.
Regarding objects that transcend the senses, such as the elements and so forth:
"The inferential means of valid cognition has been explained" (10.19).

Inference (*laiṅgika*) is said to be indirect (*parokṣa*); that by which effects such as "it will be" and so forth are understood has been explained as the means of knowledge known as inference (*anumāna*).
At the beginning of the treatise, Dharma was declared to be the subject to be explained; therefore, for the sake of recalling it, these two sūtras—which have already passed—are stated once again.

“The employment of those things seen in the Śruti and Smṛti which have a visible purpose, when that visible purpose is absent, leads to prosperity (*abhyudaya*); that is to say, it leads to *dharma*. (10.20) [76, iv] The meaning is that when there is no visible purpose for those things seen in the Śruti and Smṛti, their employment results in prosperity, i.e., in *dharma*.
And its attainment is said to be through tradition (*āmnāya*). Furthermore, the authority of tradition is established—
“The authority of tradition is due to His word” (10.21).

The Blessed Lord Īśvara is known through His being the cause of effects such as the subtle body and the world; and because He is the author of the sacred tradition (āmnāya), its authority is established. The word "iti" signifies completion. Thus, through the thorough knowledge of the similarities and differences among the categories beginning with substance, knowledge arises by way of dispassion; and from such statements as "the Self is to be known," the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa) results from the acquisition of realized wisdom through the sequence of meditative worship.

He who has always been the moon for the night of ignorance, bringing joy to this world, has composed this commentary on the *Vṛtti* [of Praśastapāda]; thus ends the *Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti* by Candrānanda.
